items.title: research-ledger: a skill that helps one person and several AI models not fool themselves
items.summary: I am not a professional researcher. I work in IT support, and in the evenings I explore ideas with several AI models: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok. Over a few months, that work produced a lot of ideas and very few results. It also showed me a pattern: the main risk was never a lack of ideas, it was fooling myself. Out of that experience came research-ledger , an MIT-licensed skill (a SKILL.md folder) that turns any assistant that reads skills into a disciplined research partner. This post explains what it does, where it came from, and what it has caught so far. The problem: four ways to fool yourself with AI Models agree with each other. Three models saying "yes, this is a real connection" feels like evidence. It isn't. They share much of their training data, so agreement is a reason to check the algebra, not a result. Metaphors dress up as mechanisms. "X in physics is like Y in learning" sounds deep. Usually nobody can write the step that actually transfers. Thresholds move after the result. A 0.62 becomes "promising" because you wanted it to be. "I didn't find it in the literature" becomes "it's new." That sentence is a statement about your search, not about the world. What the skill does idea ──► sieve (5 min) ──► translation ──► prior art ──► preregistration │ LANDED ◄────────────────┤ ▼ pilot ──► confirmatory test ──► blind round (milestones) │ ▼ DEAD · LANDED · BRIDGE CANDIDATE · BRIDGE · EXPLANATION ──► ledger Sieve first. Most ideas die in five minutes against a short checklist. They get no paperwork. Translation. Every metaphor must become a measurable test or a precise statement with a proof goal. For each analogy, the skill asks one question: mechanism or theme? If you can't write the equation or step that transfers, it's a theme. It goes into the ledger, not into an experiment. Prior art with scope. "Not found" is recorded together with the date, the search terms and the nearest source, never as novelty. Preregistration. Predictions, thresholds, controls and statistical power are frozen before the run. In a Git ledger, a separate PREREG commit pushed before the run is the proof. Pilot ≠ confirmatory test. A pilot may tune settings, but it never gives a PASS. Blind rounds. At milestones, the same seed goes to two or three models from different labs , in clean conversations, with no project context. Five verdicts. DEAD: wrong, a tautology, or killed by a control. LANDED: you rediscovered a known bridge. That's calibration, not defeat. BRIDGE CANDIDATE: known pieces, connection not found, and a new prediction. BRIDGE: only after a confirmatory test, a blind round and an independent check. EXPLANATION: a known mechanism explains the pattern. Append-only ledger. Every "no" is kept, together with what it shows and the regime where its lesson holds. Glossary. Every new term gets its standard name and a reference, or an explicit "no standard term known". A new name is not a new idea. On first use the skill asks six to eight setup questions and writes a small config: your field, where the ledger lives, which models you have for blind rounds, and how strict to be. It also asks which of your own favourite hypotheses must never be used as premises. Where the idea came from It grew out of my own log of tests, roughly forty numbered experiments so far, in toy quantum models, combinatorics, small neural networks and numerology of physical constants. Every rule in the skill is a scar from one of them. A few examples: "Zero error" can mean nothing. One model reproduced a set of measured ratios with error 0.0000. Then we ran the forgery control: random "fake" target ratios. About 3,700 formula "keys" fit the real numbers, and just as many fit the fakes. The fit was empty. That became the lock-leakage check: count how many keys fit the real lock and how many fit forged ones, before celebrating. The translator inserts what it already knows. I fed fringe and amateur texts through models to look for ideas the mainstream had missed. Most "insights" turned out to be the model translating the text into a known concept. Of the leftovers that survived translation, 6 of 8 were known science that the amateur had rediscovered. Hence the rule: check every leftover against the literature before combining it with anything. A control that can't differ from the treatment proves nothing. In a continual-learning test, the "noise control" turned out to be algebraically identical to the treatment, so the test had no power at all. The rule now: write down, before freezing, why control and treatment cannot coincide by construction. Equal strengths hide everything. Several effects worked only when all components had the same weight and vanished with heavy-tailed weights. The rule now: always retest with heavy tails. The seed style for blind rounds was added this month, after I studied the published problem prompts in openai/math . Their prompts say prove **or * refute* (never "show that"). They fix the conventions explicitly, list what is not in the setting, give no method hints and use no analogies. I adopted all of that. What it has caught (honest results) Most ideas die, and that is the method working. The ledger is mostly DEAD and LANDED entries. A pile of LANDED verdicts is useful in its own way: it measures what the translator already knows, not progress toward something new. An example of a clean kill. One idea combined local learning rules (no backpropagation) with "selectivity": only units that match the input get updated. We preregistered kill criteria and a strong control: a fly-olfaction-style model with fixed random features. The result: the selective rule made units go silent and starve, so it learned worse than updating random units; learned features beat the fixed random ones by a lot, and even a 16× wider random model stayed behind; plain feedback alignment without any gating did just as well as the gated version. So the idea is not refuted in general, but it brings nothing in that setting. Written down, with the regime, so nobody tests it again. Cross-lab review catches different things, and sometimes catches the reviewer. This week I used the method on a side project: a machine-readable atlas of proof techniques extracted from the 719 manuscripts in openai/math. Forty extracted "signatures" were reviewed blind by Claude (Anthropic) and Grok (xAI), with a frozen rubric. Grok's first attempt: 40 out of 40 "OK", every justification field empty, and in its own words "spot checks". It missed an objective error, a multiplicity of 0 where the source says 1. We marked that review invalid , not as "disagreement". Grok's second attempt, with a required quote from the source for every "OK", in four batches of ten: a real review. Agreement: the two reviewers agreed on 35 of 40 items. Each caught something the other missed: Claude was stricter on missing preconditions, Grok caught a claim taken from lines outside the cited range. Result: both reviewers passed 32 of 40 signatures (80%, 95% interval 65–90%). An earlier 6 of 10 had an interval of 31–83%, which told us almost nothing. The lesson went straight into the method: a review needs proof that the reviewer actually read the source, and planted faulty items that it must catch. A test registered before it can be contaminated. For the atlas we froze two "needs" from an open learning-theory question before anyone searched the atlas with them in mind. The test pits the atlas against plain grep on the same corpus, with a blind evaluator. My own bet, written in the preregistration: most likely undetermined . We'll see. Honest limits The method reduces self-deception. It does not produce discoveries. Blind rounds remove my context, not the models' shared training data. The checks come from a specific history. Each one is labelled with its regime, and the skill asks you to rate it useful or not for your problem instead of applying it blindly. Try it git clone https://github.com/Freeky7819/research-ledger cp -r research-ledger/research-ledger ~/.claude/skills/ It also works in Claude.ai (upload the zipped folder) and in Codex (the folder includes agents/openai.yaml ). Then just talk to it: "here's an idea…", "evaluate this paper", "this test gave 0.62, what now?", "write a blind-round seed for this". If a rule fails you, open an issue with the case. That is exactly the kind of "no" the ledger is for. Disclosure: the skill, the experiments and this post were developed together with AI models (mainly Claude, also GPT, Gemini and Grok). The questions and ideas are mine; most of the code and much of the wording were written with them.
items.summary_html:
I am not a professional researcher. I work in IT support, and in the evenings I explore ideas with several AI models: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok. Over a few months, that work produced a lot of ideas and very few results. It also showed me a pattern: the main risk was never a lack of ideas, it was fooling myself.

Out of that experience came research-ledger, an MIT-licensed skill (a SKILL.md folder) that turns any assistant that reads skills into a disciplined research partner. This post explains what it does, where it came from, and what it has caught so far.

The problem: four ways to fool yourself with AI
  1. Models agree with each other. Three models saying "yes, this is a real connection" feels like evidence. It isn't. They share much of their training data, so agreement is a reason to check the algebra, not a result.
  2. Metaphors dress up as mechanisms. "X in physics is like Y in learning" sounds deep. Usually nobody can write the step that actually transfers.
  3. Thresholds move after the result. A 0.62 becomes "promising" because you wanted it to be.
  4. "I didn't find it in the literature" becomes "it's new." That sentence is a statement about your search, not about the world.
What the skill does 
idea ──► sieve (5 min) ──► translation ──► prior art ──► preregistration
                                             │
                     LANDED ◄────────────────┤
                                             ▼
                       pilot ──► confirmatory test ──► blind round (milestones)
                                             │
                                             ▼
            DEAD · LANDED · BRIDGE CANDIDATE · BRIDGE · EXPLANATION ──► ledger
  • Sieve first. Most ideas die in five minutes against a short checklist. They get no paperwork.
  • Translation. Every metaphor must become a measurable test or a precise statement with a proof goal. For each analogy, the skill asks one question: mechanism or theme? If you can't write the equation or step that transfers, it's a theme. It goes into the ledger, not into an experiment.
  • Prior art with scope. "Not found" is recorded together with the date, the search terms and the nearest source, never as novelty.
  • Preregistration. Predictions, thresholds, controls and statistical power are frozen before the run. In a Git ledger, a separate PREREG commit pushed before the run is the proof.
  • Pilot ≠ confirmatory test. A pilot may tune settings, but it never gives a PASS.
  • Blind rounds. At milestones, the same seed goes to two or three models from different labs, in clean conversations, with no project context.
  • Five verdicts.
    • DEAD: wrong, a tautology, or killed by a control.
    • LANDED: you rediscovered a known bridge. That's calibration, not defeat.
    • BRIDGE CANDIDATE: known pieces, connection not found, and a new prediction.
    • BRIDGE: only after a confirmatory test, a blind round and an independent check.
    • EXPLANATION: a known mechanism explains the pattern.
  • Append-only ledger. Every "no" is kept, together with what it shows and the regime where its lesson holds.
  • Glossary. Every new term gets its standard name and a reference, or an explicit "no standard term known". A new name is not a new idea.

On first use the skill asks six to eight setup questions and writes a small config: your field, where the ledger lives, which models you have for blind rounds, and how strict to be. It also asks which of your own favourite hypotheses must never be used as premises.

Where the idea came from

It grew out of my own log of tests, roughly forty numbered experiments so far, in toy quantum models, combinatorics, small neural networks and numerology of physical constants. Every rule in the skill is a scar from one of them. A few examples:

  • "Zero error" can mean nothing. One model reproduced a set of measured ratios with error 0.0000. Then we ran the forgery control: random "fake" target ratios. About 3,700 formula "keys" fit the real numbers, and just as many fit the fakes. The fit was empty. That became the lock-leakage check: count how many keys fit the real lock and how many fit forged ones, before celebrating.
  • The translator inserts what it already knows. I fed fringe and amateur texts through models to look for ideas the mainstream had missed. Most "insights" turned out to be the model translating the text into a known concept. Of the leftovers that survived translation, 6 of 8 were known science that the amateur had rediscovered. Hence the rule: check every leftover against the literature before combining it with anything.
  • A control that can't differ from the treatment proves nothing. In a continual-learning test, the "noise control" turned out to be algebraically identical to the treatment, so the test had no power at all. The rule now: write down, before freezing, why control and treatment cannot coincide by construction.
  • Equal strengths hide everything. Several effects worked only when all components had the same weight and vanished with heavy-tailed weights. The rule now: always retest with heavy tails.

The seed style for blind rounds was added this month, after I studied the published problem prompts in openai/math. Their prompts say prove **or* refute* (never "show that"). They fix the conventions explicitly, list what is not in the setting, give no method hints and use no analogies. I adopted all of that.

What it has caught (honest results)

Most ideas die, and that is the method working. The ledger is mostly DEAD and LANDED entries. A pile of LANDED verdicts is useful in its own way: it measures what the translator already knows, not progress toward something new.

An example of a clean kill. One idea combined local learning rules (no backpropagation) with "selectivity": only units that match the input get updated. We preregistered kill criteria and a strong control: a fly-olfaction-style model with fixed random features. The result:

  • the selective rule made units go silent and starve, so it learned worse than updating random units;
  • learned features beat the fixed random ones by a lot, and even a 16× wider random model stayed behind;
  • plain feedback alignment without any gating did just as well as the gated version.

So the idea is not refuted in general, but it brings nothing in that setting. Written down, with the regime, so nobody tests it again.

Cross-lab review catches different things, and sometimes catches the reviewer. This week I used the method on a side project: a machine-readable atlas of proof techniques extracted from the 719 manuscripts in openai/math. Forty extracted "signatures" were reviewed blind by Claude (Anthropic) and Grok (xAI), with a frozen rubric.

  • Grok's first attempt: 40 out of 40 "OK", every justification field empty, and in its own words "spot checks". It missed an objective error, a multiplicity of 0 where the source says 1. We marked that review invalid, not as "disagreement".
  • Grok's second attempt, with a required quote from the source for every "OK", in four batches of ten: a real review.
  • Agreement: the two reviewers agreed on 35 of 40 items. Each caught something the other missed: Claude was stricter on missing preconditions, Grok caught a claim taken from lines outside the cited range.
  • Result: both reviewers passed 32 of 40 signatures (80%, 95% interval 65–90%). An earlier 6 of 10 had an interval of 31–83%, which told us almost nothing.

The lesson went straight into the method: a review needs proof that the reviewer actually read the source, and planted faulty items that it must catch.

A test registered before it can be contaminated. For the atlas we froze two "needs" from an open learning-theory question before anyone searched the atlas with them in mind. The test pits the atlas against plain grep on the same corpus, with a blind evaluator. My own bet, written in the preregistration: most likely undetermined. We'll see.

Honest limits
  • The method reduces self-deception. It does not produce discoveries.
  • Blind rounds remove my context, not the models' shared training data.
  • The checks come from a specific history. Each one is labelled with its regime, and the skill asks you to rate it useful or not for your problem instead of applying it blindly.
Try it 
git clone https://github.com/Freeky7819/research-ledger
cp -r research-ledger/research-ledger ~/.claude/skills/

It also works in Claude.ai (upload the zipped folder) and in Codex (the folder includes agents/openai.yaml). Then just talk to it: "here's an idea…", "evaluate this paper", "this test gave 0.62, what now?", "write a blind-round seed for this".

If a rule fails you, open an issue with the case. That is exactly the kind of "no" the ledger is for.

Disclosure: the skill, the experiments and this post were developed together with AI models (mainly Claude, also GPT, Gemini and Grok). The questions and ideas are mine; most of the code and much of the wording were written with them.

items.title: Show DEV: A Free Layer-Based Photo Editor That Runs Entirely in Your Browser (No Uploads)
items.summary: If you have ever tried to do "real" photo editing — layers, masks, blend modes — without a subscription, you know the usual dead ends: desktop tools cost money, and most "free online editors" quietly upload your images to a server, stamp a watermark, or cap you at three edits a day. And if you work on the web, you have probably hit a second annoyance: you just need that PNG screenshot converted to WebP or AVIF so Lighthouse stops complaining, and even that somehow requires uploading the file somewhere. I want to show you a tool that solves both problems at once. ToolsMonk's Photo Editor is a layer-based editor that runs 100% in your browser tab. Your images are opened, composited, and exported on your own device — nothing is uploaded. What you actually get (the checklist that matters) Real layers — image, text, shape, drawing, and adjustment layers, each with its own opacity, blend mode, and paintable mask Non-destructive adjustments — exposure/colour edits live on adjustment layers, so they stay reversible AI background removal and upscaling that run locally — the segmentation model executes on your device Opens HEIC — yes, those iPhone photos that half the tools on the planet refuse to open Exports PNG, JPG, WebP, AVIF, and JPEG-XL — free, no watermark, no edit cap, no signup One honest caveat: two AI features are opt-in and do touch a server — smart crop (it sends a downscaled copy) and generate image (it sends your text prompt). Everything else stays local. Four things web developers will actually use it for 1. Converting screenshots to WebP/AVIF for Core Web Vitals Drop the PNG in, export as WebP (or AVIF for even smaller sizes), done in under a minute — no upload, no command line, no "free trial expired" popup. If you want the deeper background, we wrote a full image format comparison (JPEG vs PNG vs WebP vs AVIF) and an image optimization guide for site speed . 2. Redacting client screenshots without trusting anyone Client data in a screenshot? Editing it locally means it never leaves your machine. Paint over the sensitive region on a shape layer, flatten, export. 3. Background removal for avatars and product shots The AI background removal runs the segmentation model in your browser — same category of on-device model we benchmarked in our background-removal model comparison . 4. Exam and passport photo resizing Government portals love exact pixel sizes and KB limits. Crop, resize, export as JPG under the size cap — locally. There is a full walkthrough in our exam photo & signature size guide . How it stays fast (briefly, for the curious) The whole thing is Canvas compositing: each layer is an offscreen canvas, and the editor composites the stack bottom-up with per-layer blend modes ( globalCompositeOperation ) and opacity. Adjustment layers are stored as parameters and applied at composite time — which is what keeps them reversible. No server round-trips means latency is bounded by your device, not your connection. What it deliberately does NOT do No PSD support (flatten to PNG/JPG first), no plug-ins, no CMYK/print colour management, and huge multi-layer documents are bounded by your device memory. For everyday web and document work, that trade-off is exactly why it can be free and private. Where to get it Web (no install): toolsmonk.com/tool/photo-editor Windows: Microsoft Store Android: Google Play No account, no paywall. If you hit a missing feature or a bug, the feedback link is right on the site — it's a small team and the roadmap is mostly built from those messages.

items.title: Best Enterprise AI Gateways
items.summary: TL;DR An enterprise AI gateway sits between your applications (and, increasingly, your agents and employees) and every model provider. It handles routing, failover, budgets, access control, guardrails and audit logs in one place, so you stop rebuilding them in every codebase. Judge an enterprise AI gateway on five things: overhead under real load, governance depth, where it can be deployed, MCP support, and how much of your actual AI traffic it can see. This guide compares the five leading enterprise AI gateways: Bifrost , Kong AI Gateway, Azure API Management, Portkey and LiteLLM. Bifrost is the strongest all-round enterprise AI gateway for teams that want a dedicated, self-hostable gateway with MCP governance and, through Bifrost Edge , coverage of AI tools running on employee laptops. The other four each win in a narrower situation, covered below. Two things changed this year and belong in any procurement conversation: Palo Alto Networks acquired Portkey, and LiteLLM had a PyPI supply chain incident in March. A couple of years ago, a gateway conversation meant one thing: stop pasting provider keys into config files and get a single invoice. That's still part of the job. But platform teams now get harder questions. Which MCP servers can our agents reach? Who approved them? Why did one team's spend triple in a week? And what is the sales team pasting into the desktop chat app nobody configured? An enterprise AI gateway is where those answers live, or at least where they should live. The catch is that the category has stretched. Some products are purpose-built LLM gateways, some are classic API gateways with AI policies added on top, and one just got bought by a security vendor. Picking between them on a feature checklist gets you a spreadsheet full of green ticks and no real answer. Disclosure: Bifrost is built by Maxim AI, which also publishes this blog. Weigh the ranking with that in mind. Each section below says plainly where the alternatives are the better call. What an enterprise AI gateway actually does At its core, an AI gateway is a reverse proxy for model traffic. Your apps talk to one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and the gateway translates, routes and retries across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI. What turns an AI gateway into an enterprise AI gateway is everything around that proxy: identity (SSO and roles), budgets per team or customer, audit trails you can hand to a compliance officer, deployment inside your own network, and policy that applies the same way whether the caller is a service, an autonomous agent or a person. If you want the longer version of that argument, the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide walks through the capability matrix in detail. What to check before you shortlist an enterprise AI gateway Overhead under load. Every request passes through the gateway, so its processing time is added to every model call. It's invisible on a single chat completion and very visible when an agent chains forty calls. Governance depth. Per-team budgets, rate limits, role-based access and audit logs should be enforced at the infrastructure layer, not left to each app team's good intentions. Where it runs. Regulated teams often need in-VPC, on-prem or air-gapped deployment. A gateway that only exists as a hosted service is a non-starter for them. MCP. If agents call tools, the gateway needs to control which servers and tools they can reach, and with whose credentials. Guardrails. PII redaction, secrets detection and prompt injection checks need to run before data reaches a model, with a clear choice between block, redact and log. Coverage. A gateway only governs traffic that reaches it. Ask what happens to the AI tools people install themselves. Enterprise AI gateways at a glance If you only have a minute, this is the table to read. Bifrost is the go-to enterprise AI gateway because it covers model calls, MCP tool calls and agent traffic in one gateway, runs entirely inside your own infrastructure, and is the only one here that also reaches the AI tools running on employee laptops, through Bifrost Edge . Capability Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM Form factor Standalone gateway in Go, single binary Plugins on Kong Gateway or Konnect Policies on Azure API Management Gateway plus hosted platform Python SDK and proxy Model coverage 10,000+ models, 25+ providers Major hosted and self-hosted providers Azure OpenAI plus other registered backends 1,600+ models 100+ providers Failover and balancing Weighted routing, retries, fallbacks, adaptive balancing and circuit breakers (Enterprise) Load balancing and semantic routing Backend load balancing Retries, fallbacks, load balancing Routing and fallbacks Semantic caching Yes (Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone) Yes (plugin) Yes (policies with Redis) Select Enterprise plans Yes (Qdrant, Valkey, Redis) MCP governance Native MCP gateway, tool filtering, per-user OAuth, Code Mode (up to 92.8% fewer input tokens) AI MCP Proxy and OAuth2 plugins MCP servers inside API Management MCP Gateway MCP gateway Guardrails Content safety, PII and secrets detection, plus AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR and more (Enterprise) Prompt guard plugins Content safety policy Built-in guardrails with PII detection Integrations, some need a license AI on laptops (desktop, browser, coding agents) Yes, with Bifrost Edge Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Our verdict Best all-round enterprise choice Best if Kong already runs your APIs Best for Azure-only estates Best managed option, especially for Palo Alto shops Best for Python-first teams The sections below take each gateway in turn, starting with the one we'd pick. 1. Bifrost Bifrost is an open-source (Apache 2.0) enterprise AI gateway written in Go. It gives you one OpenAI-compatible interface to 10,000+ models across 25+ providers, and the drop-in setup means moving an existing app over is a single base URL change. It ships as one binary, so it runs on a VM, Kubernetes, private cloud or a fully disconnected network, and most teams are live the same day. Speed is the headline. Bifrost's published benchmarks show about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second on a single t3.xlarge, with a 100% success rate. In the head-to-head run on AWS EC2 (500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), Bifrost sustained 424 requests per second against 44.84 for LiteLLM, with a P99 latency of 1.68 seconds versus 90.72 seconds. On the governance side, virtual keys carry budgets and rate limits that can be set per key, team, customer or model. In the Enterprise tier, governance runs off the identity provider you already use (Okta, Microsoft Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider), with SCIM 2.0 directory sync, fine-grained RBAC and data access control, and reusable access profiles so platform teams set the rules once. Routing combines weighted load balancing, retries with backoff and automatic fallbacks to another provider, and semantic caching serves stored answers to similar prompts, backed by Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate or Pinecone. // Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2024540241844224013-667'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2024540241844224013&theme=dark" } The MCP gateway is where it pulls ahead of most of this list. It governs which MCP servers and tools agents can use, with filtering at the client, request and virtual key level, and per-user OAuth so each person connects under their own account. Its Code Mode has the model write a short script to orchestrate tools instead of loading every tool definition into context, which cuts input token use by up to 92.8% across large tool sets. In a 508-tool run, Code Mode took the cost from $377 to $29 with a 100% task pass rate. The full numbers are in the MCP gateway cost and access control write-up . Then there's Bifrost Edge , which the other gateways here simply don't have an answer for. Edge runs on macOS, Windows and Linux and routes traffic from desktop chat apps, browser AI, terminal coding agents and the MCP servers they connect to through your Bifrost gateway, after a one-time SSO sign-in. Only AI traffic is routed, and nothing else on the device is inspected. The same virtual keys, budgets and guardrails apply to tools nobody wired up on purpose, with content safety, PII and secrets detection on requests and responses, plus connections to AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR, Check Point Guard and others. Admins can allow or block apps and MCP servers centrally, and a denial is enforced on the device, not just flagged in a dashboard. Rollout goes through the device management you already run: Jamf, Intune, Kandji, Omnissa Workspace ONE or JumpCloud. For regulated teams, the enterprise tier adds clustering (a peer-to-peer cluster with no leader, so an outage one node sees is acted on by all of them), adaptive load balancing with circuit breakers, signed audit logs that can't be altered, secret management through AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault, and in-VPC, on-prem or air-gapped deployment where no prompts or responses leave your infrastructure. Bifrost is SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA and GDPR compliant , and multiple Fortune 500 companies run it in production across financial services, healthcare, technology, pharmaceuticals and defense. Where to be careful: the enterprise depth (identity-based governance, clustering, adaptive load balancing, guardrail integrations, vault integrations and in-VPC deployment) sits in the paid Enterprise tier, not the open-source core. Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint, so budget for it separately, and it's still offered through early access, so pilot it on a subset of devices before a fleet-wide push. Best for : Bifrost is built for enterprises running mission-critical AI workloads that require best-in-class performance, scalability, and reliability. It serves as a centralized AI gateway to route, govern, and secure all AI traffic across models and environments with ultra low latency. Bifrost unifies LLM gateway , MCP gateway, and Agents gateway capabilities into a single platform. Designed for regulated industries and strict enterprise requirements, it supports air-gapped deployments, VPC isolation, and on-prem infrastructure. It provides full control over data, access, and execution, along with robust security, policy enforcement, and governance capabilities. 2. Kong AI Gateway Kong AI Gateway is what happens when a mature API gateway learns about LLMs. If Kong already fronts your APIs, the pitch writes itself: same control plane, same plugin model, same team on call. The AI layer adds provider routing, token-based rate limiting, prompt guard plugins, semantic caching and semantic routing across models. MCP arrived with Gateway 3.12 in October 2025. The AI MCP Proxy plugin can expose existing REST APIs as MCP tools or sit in front of an MCP server, with ACLs applied to both tool discovery and tool invocation, and a companion OAuth2 plugin handles authentication for MCP traffic. The trade-offs are practical ones. Kong's docs list the MCP plugins as part of its AI Gateway Enterprise offering, and the OAuth2 plugin was still labelled tech preview there at the time of writing. And if Kong isn't already in your stack, standing up a full API gateway platform just for LLM traffic is a lot of machinery for the job. Best for: organizations already standardized on Kong that want AI traffic on the control plane they already run. 3. Azure API Management For Azure-first companies this is the path of least resistance. Microsoft's AI gateway capabilities aren't a separate product, they're a set of policies on top of API Management. A token limit policy enforces per-consumer quotas (and can count prompt tokens up front so oversized requests never reach the backend), a metrics policy sends token usage to Application Insights, and semantic caching runs on Azure Managed Redis or another RediSearch-compatible cache. LLM backends can be load balanced, and Entra ID handles authentication. MCP support is real too. You can expose APIs as MCP servers and, per the June 2026 release notes, package them into products to control who gets what. The costs are portability and tier. Capabilities vary by API Management service tier, everything is configured through policy XML, and the whole design assumes you live in Azure. Multi-cloud or on-prem estates will feel the friction. Best for: Azure-centric enterprises with an existing API Management investment and security teams that already trust Entra and Azure Monitor. 4. Portkey (now Prisma AIRS AI Gateway) Portkey made its name as the developer-friendly managed gateway: one API for 1,600+ models, retries, fallbacks, load balancing, guardrails with PII detection, budgets, RBAC and detailed logs. It added an MCP Gateway in January 2026, the core gateway is open source, and deployment options run from SaaS to private cloud, VPC and fully self-hosted. Enterprise plans bring SAML 2.0 SSO and audit logs. The big news is ownership. Palo Alto Networks announced it would acquire Portkey and closed the deal on May 29, 2026, and the product now appears as the Prisma AIRS AI Gateway. For existing Palo Alto customers that's a neat consolidation, with the gateway sitting next to runtime security and identity tooling. For everyone else it's a fair moment to ask about roadmap and packaging, even though Palo Alto said existing and new Portkey customers will continue to be supported. One more detail: per Portkey's caching docs, semantic caching is limited to select Enterprise plans. Best for: teams that want a managed, quick-to-adopt gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem. 5. LiteLLM LiteLLM is where a lot of teams start, for good reason. It's an MIT-licensed Python SDK plus a self-hosted proxy with 100+ providers, virtual keys, budgets, routing and fallbacks, guardrails and an MCP gateway. Semantic caching works with Qdrant, Valkey or Redis, though its docs recommend keeping it to single-shot prompts and away from multi-turn agent traffic. A paid enterprise license adds SCIM, audit logs and some guardrail integrations, and Admin UI SSO is free for up to five users. Two things to weigh. First, performance: in Bifrost's published benchmarks (AWS EC2, 500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), LiteLLM sustained 44.84 requests per second with a P99 latency of 90.72 seconds, against 424 requests per second and 1.68 seconds for Bifrost. Second, supply chain hygiene. On March 24, 2026, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were published to PyPI carrying credential-stealing malware after attackers got hold of publishing credentials through a compromised CI/CD pipeline, as NetSPI's write-up describes. The bad versions were pulled. It wasn't a flaw in how the gateway works, and it could have hit any popular package. But a gateway holds every provider key you own, so pin versions and mirror packages internally whichever product you choose. Best for: Python-heavy teams with moderate traffic that value ecosystem breadth and have the capacity to run and harden a self-hosted service. Also worth a look Cloudflare AI Gateway is a solid managed option for teams already on Cloudflare, with caching, rate limiting, dynamic routing, guardrails and DLP integration. It runs on Cloudflare's network, though, so it's not an option if you need self-hosted or in-VPC. OpenRouter suits individual developers and small teams who want broad model access under one bill better than it suits governance-heavy enterprise rollouts. Enterprise controls and deployment compared This second table covers what security reviews and procurement tend to ask about when they evaluate an enterprise AI gateway: identity, audit, where the gateway runs and how it's licensed. It's where Bifrost's open-source core with an enterprise tier on top makes the most difference for regulated buyers. Control Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM SSO and roles Okta, Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider, with SCIM 2.0, RBAC and data access control (Enterprise) Kong's existing consumer and identity model Entra ID with Azure RBAC SAML 2.0 SSO and RBAC (Enterprise) Admin UI SSO free for 5 users, license beyond; SCIM with license Audit trail Signed, tamper-proof audit logs with export to S3, GCS and BigQuery (Enterprise) Kong logging plugins and Konnect analytics Azure Monitor and Application Insights Access rules and audit logs (Enterprise) Audit logs with license Where it runs Single binary: self-hosted, in-VPC, on-prem, air-gapped, clustered Self-hosted, hybrid or Konnect Azure SaaS, private cloud, VPC or self-hosted Self-hosted (Docker, Kubernetes) Licensing Apache 2.0 core plus Enterprise tier (14-day free trial); Edge priced per endpoint Open-source core, advanced AI plugins (including MCP) need a license Azure service, capabilities vary by tier Open-source gateway plus enterprise plans MIT plus enterprise license key Main trade-off Depth sits in the paid tier; Edge needs Enterprise and is in early access Needs Kong in place; MCP OAuth2 in tech preview Azure-centric, policy XML Roadmap now tied to Palo Alto Python overhead and supply chain hygiene Which AI Gateway Is Right for Your Team For teams running enterprise AI workloads with multi-provider routing, agent workflows, regulated industry compliance, or high-throughput applications, the open-source Bifrost enterprise AI gateway addresses requirements that Python-based and lighter managed gateways tend to struggle with at scale. The 11 µs overhead , native MCP gateway, hierarchical virtual key governance, and support for air-gapped and VPC deployments make it the strongest production fit where those factors matter. LiteLLM fits teams with Python-centric stacks and moderate traffic volumes that prioritize ecosystem familiarity. Kong AI Gateway fits organizations that have standardized on Kong for general API management. Azure API Management fits Azure-first estates where API Management is already approved, and Portkey fits teams that want a managed gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem. Cloudflare AI Gateway and OpenRouter fit teams with simpler requirements: managed infrastructure, lighter governance needs, or early-stage workloads that have not yet encountered the scale at which a self-hosted, compiled-language gateway becomes necessary. Teams comparing options across this range will find the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide a useful reference before finalizing a decision. Frequently asked questions What is an enterprise AI gateway? It's a control layer between AI consumers (applications, agents and employees) and model providers. It routes and retries requests across models, enforces budgets and access rules, applies guardrails, and records everything for audit, usually through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. How is an enterprise AI gateway different from an API gateway? A classic API gateway counts requests and checks auth. An AI gateway understands tokens, models and prompts: token-based budgets, failover across model vendors, semantic caching keyed on meaning, and per-model cost attribution. The line is blurrier than it used to be, since Kong and Azure API Management have added AI policies on top of their API gateways, while products like Bifrost treat those capabilities as native. Should we self-host or use a managed enterprise AI gateway? Self-hosting keeps prompts, keys and logs inside your own boundary and gives you control, in exchange for running the service. Managed options start faster but send traffic through a vendor's network. Regulated and high-volume teams usually end up self-hosted or in-VPC. Do enterprise AI gateways support MCP? All five now offer something. Bifrost has a native MCP gateway , Kong uses licensed plugins, Azure API Management exposes and packages MCP servers, Portkey has an MCP Gateway, and LiteLLM added one to its proxy. The differences are in authentication, tool-level access control and token cost, so test those rather than ticking a box. How much latency does an enterprise AI gateway add? It depends on the runtime and which features are switched on. Bifrost adds about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 RPS on a single t3.xlarge, as shown in its published benchmarks . Against model latency measured in seconds, that's noise for a single call, but overhead compounds when agents chain many calls. Can we move off LiteLLM without rewriting code? Usually yes, since both expose OpenAI-compatible APIs. Bifrost ships drop-in adapters for the LiteLLM SDK, and teams on a LiteLLM proxy can migrate models, keys, teams and users across automatically. The LiteLLM migration guide covers the cutover. Can an enterprise AI gateway govern employees using ChatGPT or Claude desktop apps? Only if that traffic reaches it. Standard gateways cover what developers deliberately route through them. Bifrost Edge closes that gap by routing desktop, browser and coding-agent traffic through the gateway so existing policies apply. Is Bifrost open source, and what does the Enterprise tier add? The core is open source under Apache 2.0 and free to self-host. The Enterprise tier adds high availability, identity-based governance, guardrail integrations, signed audit logs, vault integrations and in-VPC or air-gapped deployment, with a free 14-day trial. Bifrost Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint. Conclusion The five gateways in this comparison cover different points on the tradeoff curve between operational simplicity and production depth. For teams where AI is a core infrastructure concern, Bifrost provides the performance baseline, governance model, and enterprise deployment options that production requirements demand. To see how Bifrost fits your infrastructure, book a demo with the Bifrost team. Resources: Bifrost GitHub : https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost Bifrost Docs : https://docs.getbifrost.ai Bifrost CLI : npx -y @maximhq/bifrost-cli Thanks for reading this article! ❤️ I'd love to hear your thoughts on this mode in the comments! 💎 Check out the Bifrost repository ☆

Best for: Azure-centric enterprises with an existing API Management investment and security teams that already trust Entra and Azure Monitor.

4. Portkey (now Prisma AIRS AI Gateway)

Portkey made its name as the developer-friendly managed gateway: one API for 1,600+ models, retries, fallbacks, load balancing, guardrails with PII detection, budgets, RBAC and detailed logs. It added an MCP Gateway in January 2026, the core gateway is open source, and deployment options run from SaaS to private cloud, VPC and fully self-hosted. Enterprise plans bring SAML 2.0 SSO and audit logs.

The big news is ownership. Palo Alto Networks announced it would acquire Portkey and closed the deal on May 29, 2026, and the product now appears as the Prisma AIRS AI Gateway. For existing Palo Alto customers that's a neat consolidation, with the gateway sitting next to runtime security and identity tooling. For everyone else it's a fair moment to ask about roadmap and packaging, even though Palo Alto said existing and new Portkey customers will continue to be supported. One more detail: per Portkey's caching docs, semantic caching is limited to select Enterprise plans.

Best for: teams that want a managed, quick-to-adopt gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem.

5. LiteLLM

LiteLLM is where a lot of teams start, for good reason. It's an MIT-licensed Python SDK plus a self-hosted proxy with 100+ providers, virtual keys, budgets, routing and fallbacks, guardrails and an MCP gateway. Semantic caching works with Qdrant, Valkey or Redis, though its docs recommend keeping it to single-shot prompts and away from multi-turn agent traffic. A paid enterprise license adds SCIM, audit logs and some guardrail integrations, and Admin UI SSO is free for up to five users.

Two things to weigh. First, performance: in Bifrost's published benchmarks (AWS EC2, 500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), LiteLLM sustained 44.84 requests per second with a P99 latency of 90.72 seconds, against 424 requests per second and 1.68 seconds for Bifrost. Second, supply chain hygiene. On March 24, 2026, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were published to PyPI carrying credential-stealing malware after attackers got hold of publishing credentials through a compromised CI/CD pipeline, as NetSPI's write-up describes. The bad versions were pulled. It wasn't a flaw in how the gateway works, and it could have hit any popular package. But a gateway holds every provider key you own, so pin versions and mirror packages internally whichever product you choose.

Best for: Python-heavy teams with moderate traffic that value ecosystem breadth and have the capacity to run and harden a self-hosted service.

Also worth a look

Cloudflare AI Gateway is a solid managed option for teams already on Cloudflare, with caching, rate limiting, dynamic routing, guardrails and DLP integration. It runs on Cloudflare's network, though, so it's not an option if you need self-hosted or in-VPC. OpenRouter suits individual developers and small teams who want broad model access under one bill better than it suits governance-heavy enterprise rollouts.

Enterprise controls and deployment compared

This second table covers what security reviews and procurement tend to ask about when they evaluate an enterprise AI gateway: identity, audit, where the gateway runs and how it's licensed. It's where Bifrost's open-source core with an enterprise tier on top makes the most difference for regulated buyers.

Control Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM SSO and roles Okta, Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider, with SCIM 2.0, RBAC and data access control (Enterprise) Kong's existing consumer and identity model Entra ID with Azure RBAC SAML 2.0 SSO and RBAC (Enterprise) Admin UI SSO free for 5 users, license beyond; SCIM with license Audit trail Signed, tamper-proof audit logs with export to S3, GCS and BigQuery (Enterprise) Kong logging plugins and Konnect analytics Azure Monitor and Application Insights Access rules and audit logs (Enterprise) Audit logs with license Where it runs Single binary: self-hosted, in-VPC, on-prem, air-gapped, clustered Self-hosted, hybrid or Konnect Azure SaaS, private cloud, VPC or self-hosted Self-hosted (Docker, Kubernetes) Licensing Apache 2.0 core plus Enterprise tier (14-day free trial); Edge priced per endpoint Open-source core, advanced AI plugins (including MCP) need a license Azure service, capabilities vary by tier Open-source gateway plus enterprise plans MIT plus enterprise license key Main trade-off Depth sits in the paid tier; Edge needs Enterprise and is in early access Needs Kong in place; MCP OAuth2 in tech preview Azure-centric, policy XML Roadmap now tied to Palo Alto Python overhead and supply chain hygiene
Which AI Gateway Is Right for Your Team

For teams running enterprise AI workloads with multi-provider routing, agent workflows, regulated industry compliance, or high-throughput applications, the open-source Bifrost enterprise AI gateway addresses requirements that Python-based and lighter managed gateways tend to struggle with at scale. The 11 µs overhead, native MCP gateway, hierarchical virtual key governance, and support for air-gapped and VPC deployments make it the strongest production fit where those factors matter.

LiteLLM fits teams with Python-centric stacks and moderate traffic volumes that prioritize ecosystem familiarity. Kong AI Gateway fits organizations that have standardized on Kong for general API management. Azure API Management fits Azure-first estates where API Management is already approved, and Portkey fits teams that want a managed gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem. Cloudflare AI Gateway and OpenRouter fit teams with simpler requirements: managed infrastructure, lighter governance needs, or early-stage workloads that have not yet encountered the scale at which a self-hosted, compiled-language gateway becomes necessary. Teams comparing options across this range will find the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide a useful reference before finalizing a decision.

Frequently asked questions What is an enterprise AI gateway?

It's a control layer between AI consumers (applications, agents and employees) and model providers. It routes and retries requests across models, enforces budgets and access rules, applies guardrails, and records everything for audit, usually through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

How is an enterprise AI gateway different from an API gateway?

A classic API gateway counts requests and checks auth. An AI gateway understands tokens, models and prompts: token-based budgets, failover across model vendors, semantic caching keyed on meaning, and per-model cost attribution. The line is blurrier than it used to be, since Kong and Azure API Management have added AI policies on top of their API gateways, while products like Bifrost treat those capabilities as native.

Should we self-host or use a managed enterprise AI gateway?

Self-hosting keeps prompts, keys and logs inside your own boundary and gives you control, in exchange for running the service. Managed options start faster but send traffic through a vendor's network. Regulated and high-volume teams usually end up self-hosted or in-VPC.

Do enterprise AI gateways support MCP?

All five now offer something. Bifrost has a native MCP gateway, Kong uses licensed plugins, Azure API Management exposes and packages MCP servers, Portkey has an MCP Gateway, and LiteLLM added one to its proxy. The differences are in authentication, tool-level access control and token cost, so test those rather than ticking a box.

How much latency does an enterprise AI gateway add?

It depends on the runtime and which features are switched on. Bifrost adds about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 RPS on a single t3.xlarge, as shown in its published benchmarks. Against model latency measured in seconds, that's noise for a single call, but overhead compounds when agents chain many calls.

Can we move off LiteLLM without rewriting code?

Usually yes, since both expose OpenAI-compatible APIs. Bifrost ships drop-in adapters for the LiteLLM SDK, and teams on a LiteLLM proxy can migrate models, keys, teams and users across automatically. The LiteLLM migration guide covers the cutover.

Can an enterprise AI gateway govern employees using ChatGPT or Claude desktop apps?

Only if that traffic reaches it. Standard gateways cover what developers deliberately route through them. Bifrost Edge closes that gap by routing desktop, browser and coding-agent traffic through the gateway so existing policies apply.

Is Bifrost open source, and what does the Enterprise tier add?

The core is open source under Apache 2.0 and free to self-host. The Enterprise tier adds high availability, identity-based governance, guardrail integrations, signed audit logs, vault integrations and in-VPC or air-gapped deployment, with a free 14-day trial. Bifrost Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint.

Conclusion

The five gateways in this comparison cover different points on the tradeoff curve between operational simplicity and production depth. For teams where AI is a core infrastructure concern, Bifrost provides the performance baseline, governance model, and enterprise deployment options that production requirements demand. To see how Bifrost fits your infrastructure, book a demo with the Bifrost team.

items.title: One AGENTS.md to rule Claude Code, Cursor and Codex
items.summary: If you use more than one AI coding agent, you've probably ended up with three instruction files: a CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, a pile of .cursor/rules for Cursor, and an AGENTS.md for Codex. They start out identical. A month later one still says npm , another says pnpm , and the third forgot that tests live next to the code. That's how instruction files drift apart. The fix is simple: make AGENTS.md the single source of truth and keep every tool-specific file thin. This post shows the layout, how each tool actually picks up AGENTS.md , and a template you can copy. The layout your-repo/ ├── AGENTS.md # canonical: commands, layout, conventions, definition of done ├── CLAUDE.md # "@AGENTS.md" + Claude-only notes ├── .claude/ │ ├── settings.json # permissions + hooks │ ├── agents/ # subagents │ └── skills/ # procedures that load on demand ├── .cursor/ │ ├── rules/ # .mdc rules, with the core rule pointing at AGENTS.md │ └── cli.json # permissions for the `agent` CLI ├── .cursorignore └── .codex/ ├── config.toml # sandbox + approval defaults └── agents/ # custom agents AGENTS.md holds everything every agent needs. The other files hold only what is specific to one tool: its behaviour, permissions and features. How each tool picks up AGENTS.md This is the part people get wrong, because the three tools load it differently. Codex builds an instruction chain once per run. It starts with the global file ( ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md or AGENTS.md ), then walks every directory from the project root down to your working directory. In each one it checks AGENTS.override.md , then AGENTS.md , then any project_doc_fallback_filenames , and takes at most one file per directory. Files closer to your working directory come later, so they win when instructions conflict. The combined chain has a default size cap of 32 KiB, and Codex stops adding files once it reaches it. Cursor supports AGENTS.md in the root and in subdirectories. Nested files combine with their parents, and the more specific instructions take precedence. Claude Code has the catch. It reads AGENTS.md directly only when there's no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory or above. Once you add a CLAUDE.md , put an import at the top so both load: # CLAUDE.md @AGENTS.md A personal, uncommitted CLAUDE.local.md also counts as "a CLAUDE.md exists". So even if you never create a project CLAUDE.md , adding a local one silently stops Claude reading AGENTS.md . Keep the explicit @AGENTS.md import and that can't happen. The canonical AGENTS.md Here's a trimmed version of the template I use. Replace the placeholders with your own stack. # AGENTS.md ## Project snapshot - What it is: sentence > - Main language / runtime: 5, Node 22 > - Package manager: . Do not use any other package manager. - Layout: - `apps/web/` : frontend - `apps/api/` : HTTP API (handlers in `apps/api/src/handlers/` ) - `packages/db/` : schema + migrations ## Commands - Install: ` ` - Unit tests (fast, run often): ` ` - Single test file: ` ` - Lint + types: ` ` - Build: ` ` ## Conventions - Named exports, no default exports. - Errors: return `{ code, message }` objects from services; never throw raw strings. - New code needs tests next to it ( `*.test.ts` ). ## Working agreement 1. Restate the task in one or two lines and list the files you expect to touch before editing. 2. Make the smallest change that solves the task. No drive-by refactors. 3. If requirements are ambiguous, stop and ask. Do not guess on behaviour. 4. Never commit secrets, tokens, or `.env*` files. 5. Do not run `git push` , `git reset --hard` , `git clean -fd` , force-pushes, or destructive DB commands unless explicitly asked. ## Definition of done - [ ] Lint + types pass - [ ] Tests pass (and a new test covers the change) - [ ] Diff is limited to files related to the task - [ ] Short summary: what changed, why, how it was verified, open risks ## Code Review Rules - Flag any handler that reads request input without validation. - Flag SQL built with string concatenation. Why it's built this way Commands come first because wrong commands cause most wasted agent turns: npm instead of pnpm , or the wrong test runner. The single-file test command also saves tokens, since the agent stops running the whole suite on every iteration. The working agreement turns common failure modes, like silent scope creep and guessing, into explicit rules. The definition of done gives every agent the same exit criteria. Without it you get "Done!" while the tests still fail. ## Code Review Rules is a heading Codex's GitHub code review looks for, so the review guidance comes along for free. Keep it short. Leave formatting checks to CI, not the rule file. And write instructions the agent can verify: "Run pnpm test before finishing" works better than "test your changes". The thin files CLAUDE.md # CLAUDE.md: project instructions for Claude Code @AGENTS.md ## Claude Code specifics - Use plan mode before touching more than 3 files. - For searches that would flood the context, delegate to a subagent and ask for a summary with file paths. - Before calling a task done, run the checks in "Definition of done" and paste the command output summary. ## Things that went wrong before - Do not "fix" failing tests by loosening assertions or adding `.skip` . Two details: imports are relative to CLAUDE.md and can nest up to four hops. Block-level HTML comments are stripped before injection, so notes for humans cost no context. Run /context to confirm which memory files actually loaded. .cursor/rules/00-core.mdc Cursor project rules must be .mdc files in .cursor/rules/ . A plain .md file there is ignored. The always-on core rule just points to AGENTS.md and adds a few hard limits: --- description : " Core working agreement for every Agent chat in this repo" alwaysApply : true --- - Follow `AGENTS.md` at the repo root for commands, layout and definition of done. - Before editing, list the files you plan to change. Keep the diff limited to the task. - Never read, print, or edit `.env*` , `*.pem` , `*.key` or credential files. - Finish every task with: what changed, how you verified it (exact commands), open risks. Stack-specific rules go in separate .mdc files that attach by globs , so they only cost tokens when a matching file is in context. .codex/config.toml Codex instructions come from AGENTS.md . Behaviour (sandbox, approvals, subagents) lives in config.toml : approval_policy = "on-request" sandbox_mode = "workspace-write" web_search = "cached" [agents] max_concurrent_threads_per_session = 4 Codex loads a project's .codex/ layers only when you trust the project. When the agent "ignores" the rules If an agent ignores your conventions, the cause is almost always that the rule file is too long, vague or contradictory, or wasn't loaded at all. Check before rewriting anything: Claude Code: /context and /memory Codex: /status Cursor: Customize → Rules Then shorten the file, make the instructions verifiable, and remove conflicts. One canonical file makes that much easier, because there's only one place to fix. Wrap-up AGENTS.md is canonical. CLAUDE.md and .cursor/rules stay thin and point to it. In CLAUDE.md , always add an explicit @AGENTS.md import. Put commands first, use verifiable instructions, and give every agent the same definition of done. Keep tool behaviour (permissions, sandbox, hooks) in each tool's own config, not in the instructions. items.summary_html:
If you use more than one AI coding agent, you've probably ended up with three instruction files: a CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, a pile of .cursor/rules for Cursor, and an AGENTS.md for Codex. They start out identical. A month later one still says npm, another says pnpm, and the third forgot that tests live next to the code.

That's how instruction files drift apart. The fix is simple: make AGENTS.md the single source of truth and keep every tool-specific file thin. This post shows the layout, how each tool actually picks up AGENTS.md, and a template you can copy.

The layout 
your-repo/
├── AGENTS.md            # canonical: commands, layout, conventions, definition of done
├── CLAUDE.md            # "@AGENTS.md" + Claude-only notes
├── .claude/
│   ├── settings.json    # permissions + hooks
│   ├── agents/          # subagents
│   └── skills/          # procedures that load on demand
├── .cursor/
│   ├── rules/           # .mdc rules, with the core rule pointing at AGENTS.md
│   └── cli.json         # permissions for the `agent` CLI
├── .cursorignore
└── .codex/
    ├── config.toml      # sandbox + approval defaults
    └── agents/          # custom agents

AGENTS.md holds everything every agent needs. The other files hold only what is specific to one tool: its behaviour, permissions and features.

How each tool picks up AGENTS.md

This is the part people get wrong, because the three tools load it differently.

Codex builds an instruction chain once per run. It starts with the global file (~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md or AGENTS.md), then walks every directory from the project root down to your working directory. In each one it checks AGENTS.override.md, then AGENTS.md, then any project_doc_fallback_filenames, and takes at most one file per directory. Files closer to your working directory come later, so they win when instructions conflict. The combined chain has a default size cap of 32 KiB, and Codex stops adding files once it reaches it.

Cursor supports AGENTS.md in the root and in subdirectories. Nested files combine with their parents, and the more specific instructions take precedence.

Claude Code has the catch. It reads AGENTS.md directly only when there's no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory or above. Once you add a CLAUDE.md, put an import at the top so both load:

# CLAUDE.md
@AGENTS.md

A personal, uncommitted CLAUDE.local.md also counts as "a CLAUDE.md exists". So even if you never create a project CLAUDE.md, adding a local one silently stops Claude reading AGENTS.md. Keep the explicit @AGENTS.md import and that can't happen.

The canonical AGENTS.md

Here's a trimmed version of the template I use. Replace the placeholders with your own stack.

# AGENTS.md

## Project snapshot
- What it is:  sentence>
- Main language / runtime:  5, Node 22>
- Package manager: . Do not use any other package manager.
- Layout:
  - `apps/web/`: frontend
  - `apps/api/`: HTTP API (handlers in `apps/api/src/handlers/`)
  - `packages/db/`: schema + migrations

## Commands
- Install: ``
- Unit tests (fast, run often): ``
- Single test file: ``
- Lint + types: ``
- Build: ``

## Conventions
- Named exports, no default exports.
- Errors: return `{ code, message }` objects from services; never throw raw strings.
- New code needs tests next to it (`*.test.ts`).

## Working agreement
1. Restate the task in one or two lines and list the files you expect to touch before editing.
2. Make the smallest change that solves the task. No drive-by refactors.
3. If requirements are ambiguous, stop and ask. Do not guess on behaviour.
4. Never commit secrets, tokens, or `.env*` files.
5. Do not run `git push`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd`, force-pushes,
   or destructive DB commands unless explicitly asked.

## Definition of done
- [ ] Lint + types pass
- [ ] Tests pass (and a new test covers the change)
- [ ] Diff is limited to files related to the task
- [ ] Short summary: what changed, why, how it was verified, open risks

## Code Review Rules
- Flag any handler that reads request input without validation.
- Flag SQL built with string concatenation.
Why it's built this way
  • Commands come first because wrong commands cause most wasted agent turns: npm instead of pnpm, or the wrong test runner. The single-file test command also saves tokens, since the agent stops running the whole suite on every iteration.
  • The working agreement turns common failure modes, like silent scope creep and guessing, into explicit rules.
  • The definition of done gives every agent the same exit criteria. Without it you get "Done!" while the tests still fail.
  • ## Code Review Rules is a heading Codex's GitHub code review looks for, so the review guidance comes along for free.

Keep it short. Leave formatting checks to CI, not the rule file. And write instructions the agent can verify: "Run pnpm test before finishing" works better than "test your changes".

The thin files CLAUDE.md 
# CLAUDE.md: project instructions for Claude Code


@AGENTS.md

## Claude Code specifics
- Use plan mode before touching more than 3 files.
- For searches that would flood the context, delegate to a subagent
  and ask for a summary with file paths.
- Before calling a task done, run the checks in "Definition of done"
  and paste the command output summary.

## Things that went wrong before
- Do not "fix" failing tests by loosening assertions or adding `.skip`.

Two details: imports are relative to CLAUDE.md and can nest up to four hops. Block-level HTML comments are stripped before injection, so notes for humans cost no context. Run /context to confirm which memory files actually loaded.

.cursor/rules/00-core.mdc

Cursor project rules must be .mdc files in .cursor/rules/. A plain .md file there is ignored. The always-on core rule just points to AGENTS.md and adds a few hard limits:

---
description: "Core working agreement for every Agent chat in this repo"
alwaysApply: true
---

- Follow `AGENTS.md` at the repo root for commands, layout and definition of done.
- Before editing, list the files you plan to change. Keep the diff limited to the task.
- Never read, print, or edit `.env*`, `*.pem`, `*.key` or credential files.
- Finish every task with: what changed, how you verified it (exact commands), open risks.

Stack-specific rules go in separate .mdc files that attach by globs, so they only cost tokens when a matching file is in context.

.codex/config.toml

Codex instructions come from AGENTS.md. Behaviour (sandbox, approvals, subagents) lives in config.toml:

approval_policy = "on-request"
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
web_search = "cached"

[agents]
max_concurrent_threads_per_session = 4

Codex loads a project's .codex/ layers only when you trust the project.

When the agent "ignores" the rules

If an agent ignores your conventions, the cause is almost always that the rule file is too long, vague or contradictory, or wasn't loaded at all. Check before rewriting anything:

  • Claude Code: /context and /memory
  • Codex: /status
  • Cursor: Customize → Rules

Then shorten the file, make the instructions verifiable, and remove conflicts. One canonical file makes that much easier, because there's only one place to fix.

Wrap-up
  • AGENTS.md is canonical. CLAUDE.md and .cursor/rules stay thin and point to it.
  • In CLAUDE.md, always add an explicit @AGENTS.md import.
  • Put commands first, use verifiable instructions, and give every agent the same definition of done.
  • Keep tool behaviour (permissions, sandbox, hooks) in each tool's own config, not in the instructions.

Free excerpt: https://lirenplr.gumroad.com/l/zocmzn

items.title: Albert Heijn’s Cybersecurity Incident: Checkouts Work, but Some Distribution Centers Don’t
items.summary: Albert Heijn’s stores are open and its checkouts work. Its distribution centers are a different story. On Monday, CEO Margaret Versteden-van Duijn told NOS that work had stopped completely at some of them, because the company had switched its systems off as a precaution after a cybersecurity incident. What Ahold Delhaize Has Confirmed The disruption began on Sunday afternoon, October 11. In a statement published Monday morning, Albert Heijn said it, Etos and Gall & Gall were dealing with a cybersecurity incident and had taken immediate measures to protect their IT environment, including the temporary, precautionary shutdown of several systems. Websites, apps and customer service went offline. Logistics systems were disabled, so online grocery orders cannot be delivered until further notice. As of Monday evening, the company had not said when services would return. Inside the stores, the picture is patchy. Checkouts and this week’s national Bonus offers work. The Mijn AH app, the personal Bonus card, Koopzegels and Air Miles do not, and electronic shelf labels may still show last week’s promotional prices, which can sit below the price at the till. Albert Heijn has asked customers who miss personal discounts to keep their receipts so it can compensate them later. The problem reaches beyond the Netherlands. Parent company Ahold Delhaize said it is “experiencing a security issue within its network” and is taking some systems offline “to help protect them,” according to BleepingComputer . Grocery Dive reported that the websites of all five U.S. banners, including Food Lion, Hannaford and Stop & Shop, were down Monday morning. In Belgium, Delhaize customers could not place new orders for the week, VRT reported, although stores in Belgium and Luxembourg stayed open. The Damage Sits in the Warehouse The more consequential detail came Monday afternoon. Versteden-van Duijn told NOS that work had stopped completely in some distribution centers because “we had to switch the systems off preventively.” Albert Heijn runs six distribution centers in the Netherlands, and she would not say which ones are still working. Trade outlet Warehouse Totaal , citing RTL Z and an email sent to suppliers, reported that only the automated center in Zaandam was still running and that suppliers had been asked to deliver there within agreed time slots. Albert Heijn has not confirmed that account. Fresh food is the most exposed. Albert Heijn expects frozen goods, bread and long-life products to stay better stocked than fruit and vegetables, and says availability will vary by store. “Of course shelves will run empty if this lasts longer,” the CEO said. One delivery driver told NOS that all drivers were thrown out of the delivery app at the same time and could not log back in. The stoppage likely reflects a precaution rather than a confirmed hit on the warehouses. By the CEO’s account, the centers stopped because Albert Heijn turned its systems off, and the company has not said attackers reached them. It has also not explained why checkouts survived while logistics did not. One reading is that a store can keep selling what is already on its shelves, while a distribution center with its systems switched off cannot ship anything. That remains an inference, because the company has not described how its systems are connected. No Confirmed Data Breach, and No Quick Answer No one has said data was stolen. Albert Heijn says protecting the data of customers, employees and partners is its priority, and NOS reported that the company cannot yet say whether outsiders entered its IT systems; the CEO said the investigation is still running. Ahold Delhaize calls the event a cybersecurity incident without naming an attacker, a method or a cause, and its spokesperson did not answer whether any devices were encrypted, BleepingComputer reported. NL Times relayed RTL’s reading that the signs point to a cybercriminal attack. Neither company has confirmed that. The group’s own history argues against expecting a fast answer on data. Ahold Delhaize disclosed a cyberattack on its U.S. banners in November 2024, which halted Hannaford’s online orders for several days. It confirmed in April 2025 , about five months later, that files had been stolen, as the INC Ransom group claimed up to 6 terabytes of data from the U.S. division. Grocery Dive reports that the company later said the incident potentially exposed sensitive information of more than 2 million people. Why the Shutdown Costs So Much Shutting systems down early carries a clear defense. “The short-term pain of a planned shutdown is almost always preferable to an uncontrolled one,” said Muhammad Yahya Patel, a cybersecurity advisor at Huntress, in comments published by Cybernews . In May it told investors to expect online disruption through June and into July, and it put the hit at around £300 million for 2025/26 before mitigation, BleepingComputer reported , adding that food sales also suffered from reduced availability. Albert Heijn has not said it faces ransomware, and the M&S figures are a reference point only. Our Take : a grocer’s first-week exposure is availability. A stolen database takes months to size, as 2024 showed. A stalled distribution center shows up on shelves within days, and the products Albert Heijn flagged first, fruit and vegetables, are perishable and turn over quickly. Retail incident plans should put the restart of logistics at the center, alongside the recovery of data. Two answers will decide how this ends: whether anyone outside the company reached its systems, and how long some of its distribution centers stay shut.
