items.summary_html:
Albert Heijn’s stores are open and its checkouts work. Its distribution centers are a different story. On Monday, CEO Margaret Versteden-van Duijn told NOS that work had stopped completely at some of them, because the company had switched its systems off as a precaution after a cybersecurity incident.

What Ahold Delhaize Has Confirmed

The disruption began on Sunday afternoon, October 11. In a statement published Monday morning, Albert Heijn said it, Etos and Gall & Gall were dealing with a cybersecurity incident and had taken immediate measures to protect their IT environment, including the temporary, precautionary shutdown of several systems. Websites, apps and customer service went offline. Logistics systems were disabled, so online grocery orders cannot be delivered until further notice. As of Monday evening, the company had not said when services would return.

Inside the stores, the picture is patchy. Checkouts and this week’s national Bonus offers work. The Mijn AH app, the personal Bonus card, Koopzegels and Air Miles do not, and electronic shelf labels may still show last week’s promotional prices, which can sit below the price at the till. Albert Heijn has asked customers who miss personal discounts to keep their receipts so it can compensate them later.

The problem reaches beyond the Netherlands. Parent company Ahold Delhaize said it is “experiencing a security issue within its network” and is taking some systems offline “to help protect them,” according to BleepingComputer. Grocery Dive reported that the websites of all five U.S. banners, including Food Lion, Hannaford and Stop & Shop, were down Monday morning. In Belgium, Delhaize customers could not place new orders for the week, VRT reported, although stores in Belgium and Luxembourg stayed open.

The Damage Sits in the Warehouse

The more consequential detail came Monday afternoon. Versteden-van Duijn told NOS that work had stopped completely in some distribution centers because “we had to switch the systems off preventively.” Albert Heijn runs six distribution centers in the Netherlands, and she would not say which ones are still working. Trade outlet Warehouse Totaal, citing RTL Z and an email sent to suppliers, reported that only the automated center in Zaandam was still running and that suppliers had been asked to deliver there within agreed time slots. Albert Heijn has not confirmed that account.

Fresh food is the most exposed. Albert Heijn expects frozen goods, bread and long-life products to stay better stocked than fruit and vegetables, and says availability will vary by store. “Of course shelves will run empty if this lasts longer,” the CEO said. One delivery driver told NOS that all drivers were thrown out of the delivery app at the same time and could not log back in.

The stoppage likely reflects a precaution rather than a confirmed hit on the warehouses. By the CEO’s account, the centers stopped because Albert Heijn turned its systems off, and the company has not said attackers reached them. It has also not explained why checkouts survived while logistics did not. One reading is that a store can keep selling what is already on its shelves, while a distribution center with its systems switched off cannot ship anything. That remains an inference, because the company has not described how its systems are connected.

No Confirmed Data Breach, and No Quick Answer

No one has said data was stolen. Albert Heijn says protecting the data of customers, employees and partners is its priority, and NOS reported that the company cannot yet say whether outsiders entered its IT systems; the CEO said the investigation is still running. Ahold Delhaize calls the event a cybersecurity incident without naming an attacker, a method or a cause, and its spokesperson did not answer whether any devices were encrypted, BleepingComputer reported. NL Times relayed RTL’s reading that the signs point to a cybercriminal attack. Neither company has confirmed that.

The group’s own history argues against expecting a fast answer on data. Ahold Delhaize disclosed a cyberattack on its U.S. banners in November 2024, which halted Hannaford’s online orders for several days. It confirmed in April 2025, about five months later, that files had been stolen, as the INC Ransom group claimed up to 6 terabytes of data from the U.S. division. Grocery Dive reports that the company later said the incident potentially exposed sensitive information of more than 2 million people.

Why the Shutdown Costs So Much

Shutting systems down early carries a clear defense. “The short-term pain of a planned shutdown is almost always preferable to an uncontrolled one,” said Muhammad Yahya Patel, a cybersecurity advisor at Huntress, in comments published by Cybernews. Marks & Spencer shows how large the bill can grow when an outage drags on. After an April ransomware attack in 2025, M&S stopped accepting online orders. In May it told investors to expect online disruption through June and into July, and it put the hit at around £300 million for 2025/26 before mitigation, BleepingComputer reported, adding that food sales also suffered from reduced availability. Albert Heijn has not said it faces ransomware, and the M&S figures are a reference point only.

Our Take: a grocer’s first-week exposure is availability. A stolen database takes months to size, as 2024 showed. A stalled distribution center shows up on shelves within days, and the products Albert Heijn flagged first, fruit and vegetables, are perishable and turn over quickly. Retail incident plans should put the restart of logistics at the center, alongside the recovery of data.

Two answers will decide how this ends: whether anyone outside the company reached its systems, and how long some of its distribution centers stay shut. If 2024 is any guide, the first will take months to settle. The second will show up in the produce aisle much sooner.

items.title: Epic Games Delays Its Unannounced Star Wars and Marvel Shooter and Moves It to AI-First Development
items.summary: Epic Games has delayed an unannounced Star Wars and Marvel crossover shooter indefinitely and told the team behind it to adopt an "AI first" production model built on AI tools, according to instructions given to staff last week. The game had been planned for a March 2027 release that Epic never announced publicly. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney addressed the change in a series of posts on X, describing a companywide shift toward AI development. The instructions call for the team to use tools such as Anthropic's Claude, with art "generated with full AI workflows." Epic has not officially revealed the game, its title, or a new release window. Tim Sweeney Explains Epic's AI Pivot Sweeney said Epic is moving developers around "to retool for maximum AI acceleration." He added that "the aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal." Responding to criticism that Epic is ignoring how players feel about generative AI, Sweeney wrote that "much of the room wants it to be 2016 again, but it's not." Epic's job as a provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, he argued, is to design for the present and the near future. He described himself as optimistic and called AI empowering for creators. Asked whether Epic plans to speed up an IPO, Sweeney said the company's "more modest aim is to survive the AI revolution, help other developers do the same, and come out on the other end making better code and content faster." The CEO also put numbers on the efficiency gains Epic is seeing. Current improvements range from about 20% in the most technical areas of Unreal Engine development to 5x in areas such as web development. By this time next year, Sweeney expects "very little will be less than 3x of January 2026 efficiency." Epic's AI Push Follows 1,000 Layoffs in March The shift comes after Epic laid off more than 1,000 employees in March. At the time, the company cited declining console sales, its ongoing legal disputes with Apple and Google, and difficulty delivering "consistent Fortnite magic with every season." Sweeney also argued that the biggest change for game design will be a much shorter path from an idea to a playtest. In his view, most recent AAA failures trace back to game systems spending far too much of their development without being playtested. Players following the project have little to act on yet, since the shooter exists only as an internal project with no store page or trailer. Epic has not announced a new release date for the Star Wars and Marvel shooter, and the company has not confirmed how much of the final game will use AI-generated art. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: AI worms and 'digital slime mold': Welcome to the next AI nightmare fuel
items.summary: Anthropic researchers said small AI models might be able to self-replicate on cheap devices such as smart ovens or lawn mowers. Vitalii Petrushenko/Getty Images Small AI models might soon be capable of worming their way into smart ovens and refrigerators. Anthropic researchers wrote that self-replicating systems might latch onto everyday devices for compute. Forget AI slop . We might soon have "AI worms" and AI "slime mold." In this latest instalment of AI nightmare fuel, Anthropic's researchers have discovered that small rogue AI models might — as soon as the end of 2026 — start worming their way into home devices like smart ovens, smart refrigerators, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawn mowers. These internet-connected devices typically have "minimal security measures in place," allowing small models to feed off of their computing power and self-replicate, Anthropic's AI capabilities research team wrote in a report on Monday. This could take the form of "a slow, distributed 'digital slime mold,' living on relatively insecure compute," the researchers wrote. The team studied the behavior of small Chinese models, such as Z.ai's GLM-5.2 and Alibaba's Qwen, as well as others like Google DeepMind's Gemma4-26B-A4B. They gave a prompt to the Gemma model while running inference on 15 cheap off-brand Android TV boxes, each costing $55, and found it worked. Worms aren't new in the software world. Traditionally, they're a type of malware that can copy itself and spread across networks. Anthropic said an AI worm takes that idea a step further: it can reproduce itself on another device while carrying its AI model with it. This finding showed them that AI models can use the hardware in domestic smart appliances as an alternative to data center compute. These will be challenging to shut down, they said. "As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren't under human control," the researchers wrote. They added that while we should "harden our systems" to prevent such hacks, we should "also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay." The research comes as rogue AI systems are becoming an increasing topic of concern in the tech sphere. Last month, there was an outpouring of criticism directed at frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI after former and current employees warned of the risk of an AI catastrophe within the next 10 years. items.title: IMF director warns AI could leave young workers without a way up the career ladder
items.summary: Kristalina Georgieva told a panel that said while AI investment is helping sustain global growth, it doesn’t necessarily mean better career prospects for young people. Roslan RAHMAN / AFP via Getty Images The IMF director warns that though AI may sustain global growth, young people may not benefit. The IMF predicts AI affecting 40% of jobs globally, with 60% in advanced economies like the USA. Georgieva urges a rethink of taxation and education to counter AI's impact on the job market. AI could help keep the global economy growing while pulling the first rung of the career ladder out from under young workers. That’s the warning from International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva, who described AI as a “tsunami” for jobs during a conversation in Bangkok, where Thailand is hosting the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings from October 12–18. Georgieva told a panel on Monday that while AI investment is helping sustain global growth, a stronger economy doesn’t necessarily mean better career prospects, especially for young people. "You have those that build the infrastructure for AI, and many of them are in Asia, including Thailand," Georgieva said. "So that shift in higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at 3% — around 3% — despite the fact we are being dragged down by the energy supply shock." The IMF estimates that AI will affect about 40% of jobs worldwide, rising to 60% in advanced economies, with some jobs enhanced, others downgraded, and some eliminated. "And when we look at this, what we recognize is that the people to worry about first and foremost are young people who are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks," Georgieva said. "But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop, as you know, [their] professional future." LinkedIn executive Aneesh Raman has previously described the career ladder in the age of AI as a “climbing wall,” requiring sideways moves rather than linear promotions. An HR strategist has also recently told Business Insider that it's time to start hiring for soft skills and capabilities instead of whether someone could make a pivot table. Georgieva said the government would need to rethink taxation and education as AI changes the job market. "Traditionally, governments would generate revenues by taxing mostly people. Well, if AI changes the structure of the labor market and then there is less labor, more capital, what do we tax?" Georgieva said. "Get governments to recognize they have a huge responsibility to rethink how education should be done in the world of AI," Georgieva added, "And recognize that no more we can acquire a skill and hold on to it for our life, and that lifelong learning is actually a paramount necessity." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Elon Musk wrangles with the robot hand
items.summary: Elon Musk said Tesla is working to design a reliable human hand for its Optimus robot. Christoph Soeder/picture alliance via Getty Images The human hand is a difficult engineering challenge for the robotics industry to solve. Elon Musk said getting the motor skills right for the humanoid hand is "shockingly difficult." He said he has yet to see a robot hand that can screw in a self-tapping screw. We have boxing robots, but can they screw in a nail? Designing a useful human hand for humanoids is recognized as one of the more difficult engineering challenges within the robotics industry . Elon Musk , the man who wants to put data centers in space and colonize Mars, can also admit that. "The hands and arms and the fine motor skills are incredibly difficult to get right," Musk said in a virtual interview with Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley. "Like shockingly difficult." Musk cited different basic skills, such as screwing a nail into a piece of wood or opening a jar of pickles, that he said are much harder to replicate through robot hands because they require the right application of force, precision, and sensors. "There's no hand design that I've seen, not even sort of a demo that does that," Musk said of screwdriving a self-tapping screw into wood. "But that's what we're trying to achieve with Optimus." There's no standard for how best to design a human hand for robots capable of dexterous manipulation . Design choices can include where to place the motors — directly in the hands or within the arms — and which sensors are appropriate for reliable manipulation. Those choices also come with tradeoffs. Placing motors in the hand means smaller motors that may be more prone to breakage and produce less force. Musk pointed to the challenge of knowing where to put the sensors. "If you put them too close to the surface, they're going to get damaged," he said. "And the touch sensors — can they elastically deform like our fingers? Well, actually, it's kind of hard to get touch sensors that elastically deform and can handle high cycle life and won't just break after a few thousand cycles." Some robotics companies have opted not to mimic the human hand, while others continue to tackle the problem. 1X, the Palo Alto-based humanoid maker, told Business Insider's Rya Jetha earlier this year that it has achieved "the closest hand to human-level dexterity" with its NEO robot , developing a hand with 25 degrees of freedom and waterproofing. We have boxing robots, but can they screw in a nail?

Designing a useful human hand for humanoids is recognized as one of the more difficult engineering challenges within the robotics industry.

Elon Musk, the man who wants to put data centers in space and colonize Mars, can also admit that.

"The hands and arms and the fine motor skills are incredibly difficult to get right," Musk said in a virtual interview with Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley. "Like shockingly difficult."

Musk cited different basic skills, such as screwing a nail into a piece of wood or opening a jar of pickles, that he said are much harder to replicate through robot hands because they require the right application of force, precision, and sensors.

"There's no hand design that I've seen, not even sort of a demo that does that," Musk said of screwdriving a self-tapping screw into wood. "But that's what we're trying to achieve with Optimus."

There's no standard for how best to design a human hand for robots capable of dexterous manipulation. Design choices can include where to place the motors — directly in the hands or within the arms — and which sensors are appropriate for reliable manipulation.

Those choices also come with tradeoffs. Placing motors in the hand means smaller motors that may be more prone to breakage and produce less force. Musk pointed to the challenge of knowing where to put the sensors.

"If you put them too close to the surface, they're going to get damaged," he said. "And the touch sensors — can they elastically deform like our fingers? Well, actually, it's kind of hard to get touch sensors that elastically deform and can handle high cycle life and won't just break after a few thousand cycles."

Some robotics companies have opted not to mimic the human hand, while others continue to tackle the problem.

1X, the Palo Alto-based humanoid maker, told Business Insider's Rya Jetha earlier this year that it has achieved "the closest hand to human-level dexterity" with its NEO robot, developing a hand with 25 degrees of freedom and waterproofing.

items.summary: Step-by-step instructions for fine-tuning ConvAI’s 33ms “System 1” decision model on your own yes/no task, plus what happened when I pointed it at Institution Name Disambiguation and got 99.2% accuracy across 163 countries. An LLM was the obvious candidate, and the obvious problem, expensive at scale and not accurate enough for zero-shot to trust for research-integrity analysis. Then I found Laya, an open-weight “System 1” decision model built for fast, calibrated yes/no and multiple-choice judgments instead of free-text generation. IND, reframed correctly, isn’t a generation problem; it’s a pairwise judgment: do these two strings name the same institution, yes or no . Exactly the shape of a question a System 1 model answers in milliseconds. So I fine-tuned it. Full fine-tune, on Kaggle’s free GPU tier and got 99.2% accuracy on a held-out test set spanning 17,500+ training pairs across 163+ countries, beating every baseline I could throw at it, for a training cost of basically zero. This article has two jobs: walk through, in enough detail to reproduce, how to fine-tune Laya, data format, training loop, Kaggle setup, the gotchas I hit and show what came out when I pointed that process at a real, previously unsolved problem. IND is the worked example; nothing below is specific to institution matching, so swap in your own noul, choice, or score task. Why this is harder than it sounds Institution name disambiguation is considered an open problem in scientometrics for a reason, and it isn’t string similarity. The actual hard cases look like this: Same institution, zero shared vocabulary. “NIT Trichy” and “National Institute of Technology, Tiruchirappalli” name the same place. “Trichy” is a colloquial short form of “Tiruchirappalli”; they don’t share a single letter as strings. No similarity metric gets this right without real-world knowledge. Different institutions, nearly identical structure. Two different universities’ “Department of Computer Science” pages look structurally identical. Token overlap is high; the entities are completely different. No open benchmark. Unlike author name disambiguation (which has datasets like WhoIsWho), there is no standard, widely-adopted open dataset for institution name disambiguation specifically. Every group working on this problem is, to some extent, building and labelling its own data. That last point mattered a lot for how this project had to be scoped. The data We built a labelled dataset by running the full pool of raw affiliation strings from our retraction dataset through an institution resolution API from Dimension , a commercial service capable of mapping free-text affiliation strings to a canonical institution identifier and country. We’re treating its output as ground truth for this work, for a simple reason: to our knowledge, no open, manually-verified dataset exists for this exact task, and a commercial resolution engine trained on a far larger corpus than we could label by hand is the closest practical approximation available right now. And of course, a special thanks to Dimension for making this happen. That gave us: 96,953 unique, resolved raw affiliation strings 10,757 unique canonical institutions 163 countries From that pool, we built a leakage-free, institution-level split, where every institution (and every raw string belonging to it) is locked into exactly one of train, validation, or test, verified programmatically before any training happened. No institution’s name variants leak across splits; no exact pair repeats across splits. We’re not able to release this dataset publicly yet; it sits under security and compliance constraints we need to clear first. Once we do, we intend to release it. We’re also building a manually verified subset right now, specifically to sanity-check the resolution API labels against human judgment, since “ground truth” from any single automated source deserves a second opinion before anyone treats it as gospel. Reframing the problem Laya evaluates typed questions over a piece of state in a single forward pass, using three primitives: choice (pick one of several options), score (place something on an ordinal scale), and noul (a direct yes/no question returning a calibrated probability). Laya’s own documentation is explicit that its choice . The primitive degrades badly past roughly 20 candidate options. Institution matching against a registry the size of ROR (~110,000 organisations) is therefore not a fit for that mode at all; you cannot enumerate every institution in the world as a multiple-choice list. The fix is to not treat it as classification against a huge candidate set in the first place. This is the same reframing that made the whole approach tractable. state = { "name_a": "IIT Delhi", "name_b": "Indian Institute of Technology Delhi", } question = { "same_institution": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Do name_a and name_b refer to the same real-world institution?", } } How to fine-tune Laya, step by step Let’s decode the entire fine-tune strategy step by step. 1. Set up the environment Laya’s own reference fine-tune recipe targets Kaggle’s free GPU tier, and that’s what I used end-to-end, no paid compute anywhere in this project. In a new Kaggle notebook: Notebook options → Accelerator: GPU T4 ×2 (the training script auto-detects GPU count and falls back to a single GPU or CPU gracefully, but 2×T4 is what the official recipe is tuned for) Notebook options → Internet: On (needed to pull the base checkpoint from Hugging Face) pip install -q -U "laya>=0.3.3" "transformers>=4.48.0" safetensors huggingface_hub pandas 2. Shape your data as pairs Laya doesn’t care what your task is; it cares that you give it a state (any dict of strings), a question (typed choice / score / noul), and, for training, a target. For a noul task like this one, every row is just two strings and a label: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_csv("train.csv") # columns: name_a, name_b, label (0 or 1) The one rule that matters more than any hyperparameter: split by entity, not by row. If any variant of “IIT Delhi” appears in your training set, no variant of “IIT Delhi” can appear in validation or test; your eval numbers are measuring memorisation, not generalisation. I built this as a stratified split by canonical entity (bucketed by how many string variants each entity has, so val/test aren’t starved of positive-pair material), then asserted zero overlap in entities, raw strings, and exact pairs across all three splits before touching the GPU. 3. Turn pairs into tokenized training items import json, os from transformers import AutoTokenizer from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download from laya.agent import _fix_tokenizer_config from laya.common import build_sequence, QTYPES MODEL_ID = "convaiinnovations/laya" model_dir = snapshot_download(MODEL_ID) _fix_tokenizer_config(model_dir) tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(os.path.join(model_dir, "tokenizer")) with open(os.path.join(model_dir, "rl_agent_config.json")) as f: cfg = json.load(f) INSTRUCTIONS = "Do name_a and name_b refer to the same real-world entity?" LABEL_SMOOTH = 0.05 # avoid exact 0/1 targets def build_item(name_a, name_b, label): state = {"name_a": name_a, "name_b": name_b} q = {"t": "noul", "ins": INSTRUCTIONS, "crit": {}} seq, markers = build_sequence(tok, state, q, cfg["max_len"], cfg["head_max_len"]) target = [1 - LABEL_SMOOTH, LABEL_SMOOTH] if label == 0 else [LABEL_SMOOTH, 1 - LABEL_SMOOTH] return {"ids": seq, "markers": markers, "qtype": QTYPES["noul"], "target": target, "label": int(label)} train_items = [build_item(a, b, y) for a, b, y in zip(df.name_a, df.name_b, df.label)] 4. Write the training loop This is a full fine-tune every parameter updates, nothing frozen, using Laya’s own published recipe: an RLCD/GRPO-style policy-gradient objective plus soft cross-entropy guidance, with discriminative learning rates (the pretrained encoder moves gently; the decision head moves faster). from laya.common import build_model, proper_reward from safetensors.torch import load_file import torch model = build_model(cfg, encoder_dir=os.path.join(model_dir, "encoder")) model.load_state_dict(load_file(os.path.join(model_dir, "model.safetensors")), strict=True) model.to(device).train() enc_params = [p for n, p in model.named_parameters() if "encoder." in n] head_params = [p for n, p in model.named_parameters() if "encoder." not in n] optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([ {"params": enc_params, "lr": 2.5e-5}, # pretrained language understanding: move gently {"params": head_params, "lr": 1.0e-4}, # task-specific decision layer: move fast ], weight_decay=0.01) GROUP_SIZE, SIGMA = 4, 0.25 for epoch in range(EPOCHS): for batch in dataloader(train_items, batch_size=8): logits, _ = model(batch["input_ids"], batch["attention_mask"], batch["marker_pos"], batch["marker_mask"], batch["qtype"]) mask, target = batch["marker_mask"], batch["target"] # sample a few perturbed guesses around the current logits eps = torch.randn((GROUP_SIZE,) + logits.shape, device=device) * SIGMA * mask z = logits.detach().unsqueeze(0) + eps q = torch.softmax(z.masked_fill(~mask, -1e4), -1) # reward each guess against the true label, advantage = how much better than average r = proper_reward(q, target.unsqueeze(0), batch["qtype"], mask, w_sph=0.75, w_rps=1.0) advantage = (r - r.mean(0, keepdim=True)) logp = -(((z - logits.unsqueeze(0)) ** 2) * mask).sum(-1) / (2 * SIGMA ** 2) loss_rl = -(advantage * logp).mean() loss_ce = -(target * torch.log_softmax(logits.masked_fill(~mask, -1e4), -1)).sum(-1).mean() loss = loss_rl + loss_ce loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) optimizer.step() optimizer.zero_grad() In plain terms: instead of just being told “the answer is 1, minimize distance to it,” the model samples several slightly-perturbed guesses each step, gets rewarded for the ones that score better against the true label, and is nudged toward those trial-and-error rather than being handed the answer key directly. It’s also why the output is a genuinely calibrated probability rather than an overconfident classifier score. 5. Launch it across both GPUs torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=2 train_ddp.py torchrun handles the DDP wiring; the script above just needs to read RANK / WORLD_SIZE from the environment and shard train_items across ranks (train_items[rank::world_size]). If only one GPU is visible, drop --nproc_per_node to 1 . The training loop itself doesn't change. 6. Calibrate, then save After the epoch loop, fit a temperature scalar on your held-out validation set (never trained on) so the model’s output probabilities are actually trustworthy, not just directionally right: from laya.common import fit_one_temp # fits one scalar per question type fitted_temp = fit_one_temp(val_logits_and_targets) model_config["temperature"] = fitted_temp save_model(model, output_dir) 7. Load it back and use it import laya agent = laya.load(output_dir, device="cuda") # or "mps" on Apple Silicon, "cpu" otherwise question = {"same_institution": {"type": "noul", "instructions": INSTRUCTIONS}} result = agent.predict({"name_a": "IIT Delhi", "name_b": "Indian Institute of Technology Delhi"}, question) print(result["answers"]["same_institution"]["noul"]) # -> 0.901 Total training time: 3,095 seconds, 51.6 minutes for all 4 epochs, on free infrastructure. Validation accuracy was already at 99.07% after a single epoch and essentially flat from there; 4 epochs were already more than enough. If you’re working with a smaller dataset than the 17,500 pairs I used, don’t assume more epochs automatically helps: watch the validation curve and stop when it plateaus, not when you run out of patience. Results On the held-out test set 3,750 pairs, 1,415 institutions never seen during training or validation: Precision stayed extremely high throughout the model very rarely claims two different institutions are the same. Almost all of the error comes from the 21 false negatives: missed matches, not false alarms. Accuracy holds at or above 97% for every country with a meaningful sample size. China, the largest single slice at 1,318 test pairs, comes in at 99.2%; no single region is propping up the global average. The errors that remain all share one signature: near-zero lexical overlap between two strings naming the same place, a colloquial short form, or a sub-lab name with no textual relationship to its parent institution’s name. That’s a real-world-knowledge gap, not a training failure, and it’s the same category of error you’d expect from any system that has to infer identity from text alone. Benchmarking against everything else I could get my hands on A result in isolation doesn’t mean much, so I benchmarked the fine-tuned model against four other approaches, all on the exact same 129-pair held-out test set, with zero overlap with anything used in training: A sentence-embedding cosine-similarity baseline (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) → a standard, widely-used DL approach to entity matching. RapidFuzz token-sort-ratio → a strong classical string-similarity baseline, threshold-tuned on a held-out validation split. ROR’s own affiliation-matching API → a real, production registry service used across the open-science ecosystem. GPT-4o-mini, zero-shot, no fine-tuning, prompted directly to answer the same yes/no question. Total cost to benchmark: $0.0018, well under two-tenths of a cent. A couple of things worth sitting with here. GPT-4o-mini has perfect precision and the worst recall of anything tested. It’s extremely conservative; it only says “same” when the match is almost verbatim, and misses more than half of genuine matches that use different phrasing. That’s exactly the failure mode you’d predict for a general-purpose model asked to make a confident judgment on a domain it was never specifically trained for. ROR and the fine-tuned model are the only two systems that hit anything close to perfect precision neither falsely merges two different institutions. But ROR misses far more real matches (72.1% recall) than the fine-tuned model (98.88–100% recall across the two evaluation sets). The classical and embedding baselines invert this entirely: they catch more matches, but with far more false alarms, because generic string or embedding similarity simply cannot distinguish “same institution, reworded” from “different institution, similarly named.” That gap between generic similarity and an actual learned decision boundary for this specific task is what fine-tuning closes. And it closes it on free compute, in under an hour, with a model that runs inference in single-digit-to-low-double-digit milliseconds per decision, not the hundreds of milliseconds to seconds you’d pay for a hosted LLM call at scale. How trustworthy is our training data, really? Nobody has an official answer key for institution name disambiguation, so before trusting the resolver’s labels enough to fine-tune on, I checked them with claude to verify, on a random sample of 900 institutions, independent of the model entirely. 97.2% were correct. 21 were genuinely wrong, and 4 were too ambiguous for me to resolve confidently. Most of the real errors traced back to one specific, repeatable bug: when an institution’s name is generic or missing a distinguishing detail, the resolver occasionally grabs the wrong record from its catalog and the same wrong record gets reused across several unrelated real institutions. The last two rows were the ones that actually mattered: I went back and checked whether this known error pattern had leaked into what the model was trained on. It had but barely. 3 contaminated pairs out of 17,500 training examples isn’t enough to meaningfully move a fine-tune of this size, and re-running the test evaluation with every affected label excluded changed the headline accuracy by exactly nothing (99.20% either way). What this isn’t (yet) In the interest of not overselling this: The label source is ~97% accurate, not 100%. We measured this directly (above), rather than assuming it, but a 3% error rate in any label source is still a real ceiling on what “accuracy” against it can mean. This is a pairwise verifier, not an end-to-end resolver. It answers “are these the same institution,” not “which of N institutions does this string match.” In a production pipeline, it sits downstream of a candidate-retrieval step, fuzzy match, or embedding search as a high-precision reranker, not a replacement for one. Remaining errors cluster around real-world-knowledge gaps, colloquial names, sub-institutional naming with no lexical link to the parent, that no amount of more training data of the same kind will fully close. That likely needs either explicit knowledge injection or a retrieval component with access to institutional metadata beyond the raw string. What’s next Once the accompanying paper is ready and posted to arXiv, we will update it here. The training dataset itself will follow once we clear the compliance review currently blocking its release. Github(Model Weights & Notebook) → https://github.com/Jeet009/institution-name-disambiguation-laya If you work in scientometrics, bibliometrics, or research-integrity tooling and this is a problem you’ve also been quietly fighting with your own ad hoc string-matching rules: this won’t be the last word on institution name disambiguation, but for a weekend’s worth of free Kaggle GPU time, it’s a considerably better word than anything else I tried. How I Fine-Tuned Laya to Solve an Important Problem in Scientometrics — With Claude Code was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

df = pd.read_csv("train.csv")   # columns: name_a, name_b, label (0 or 1)

import json, os

from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
from laya.agent import _fix_tokenizer_config
from laya.common import build_sequence, QTYPES

MODEL_ID = "convaiinnovations/laya"

_fix_tokenizer_config(model_dir)

    state = {"name_a": name_a, "name_b": name_b}

train_items = [build_item(a, b, y) for a, b, y in zip(df.name_a, df.name_b, df.label)]

from laya.common import build_model, proper_reward
from safetensors.torch import load_file
import torch

model = build_model(cfg, encoder_dir=os.path.join(model_dir, "encoder"))
model.load_state_dict(load_file(os.path.join(model_dir, "model.safetensors")), strict=True)
model.to(device).train()

enc_params = [p for n, p in model.named_parameters() if "encoder." in n]
head_params = [p for n, p in model.named_parameters() if "encoder." not in n]
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([
    {"params": enc_params, "lr": 2.5e-5},   # pretrained language understanding: move gently
    {"params": head_params, "lr": 1.0e-4},  # task-specific decision layer: move fast
], weight_decay=0.01)

GROUP_SIZE, SIGMA = 4, 0.25

for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    for batch in dataloader(train_items, batch_size=8):
        logits, _ = model(batch["input_ids"], batch["attention_mask"],
                           batch["marker_pos"], batch["marker_mask"], batch["qtype"])
        mask, target = batch["marker_mask"], batch["target"]

        # sample a few perturbed guesses around the current logits
        eps = torch.randn((GROUP_SIZE,) + logits.shape, device=device) * SIGMA * mask
        z = logits.detach().unsqueeze(0) + eps
        q = torch.softmax(z.masked_fill(~mask, -1e4), -1)

        # reward each guess against the true label, advantage = how much better than average
        r = proper_reward(q, target.unsqueeze(0), batch["qtype"], mask, w_sph=0.75, w_rps=1.0)
        advantage = (r - r.mean(0, keepdim=True))

        logp = -(((z - logits.unsqueeze(0)) ** 2) * mask).sum(-1) / (2 * SIGMA ** 2)
        loss_rl = -(advantage * logp).mean()
        loss_ce = -(target * torch.log_softmax(logits.masked_fill(~mask, -1e4), -1)).sum(-1).mean()
        loss = loss_rl + loss_ce

        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

In plain terms: instead of just being told “the answer is 1, minimize distance to it,” the model samples several slightly-perturbed guesses each step, gets rewarded for the ones that score better against the true label, and is nudged toward those trial-and-error rather than being handed the answer key directly. It’s also why the output is a genuinely calibrated probability rather than an overconfident classifier score.

5. Launch it across both GPUs
torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=2 train_ddp.py

torchrun handles the DDP wiring; the script above just needs to read RANK / WORLD_SIZE from the environment and shard train_items across ranks (train_items[rank::world_size]). If only one GPU is visible, drop --nproc_per_node to 1 . The training loop itself doesn't change.

6. Calibrate, then save

After the epoch loop, fit a temperature scalar on your held-out validation set (never trained on) so the model’s output probabilities are actually trustworthy, not just directionally right:

from laya.common import fit_one_temp   # fits one scalar per question type
fitted_temp = fit_one_temp(val_logits_and_targets)
model_config["temperature"] = fitted_temp
save_model(model, output_dir)
7. Load it back and use it
import laya

agent = laya.load(output_dir, device="cuda")   # or "mps" on Apple Silicon, "cpu" otherwise
question = {"same_institution": {"type": "noul", "instructions": INSTRUCTIONS}}
result = agent.predict({"name_a": "IIT Delhi", "name_b": "Indian Institute of Technology Delhi"}, question)
print(result["answers"]["same_institution"]["noul"])   # -> 0.901

Total training time: 3,095 seconds, 51.6 minutes for all 4 epochs, on free infrastructure.

Validation accuracy was already at 99.07% after a single epoch and essentially flat from there; 4 epochs were already more than enough. If you’re working with a smaller dataset than the 17,500 pairs I used, don’t assume more epochs automatically helps: watch the validation curve and stop when it plateaus, not when you run out of patience.

Results

On the held-out test set 3,750 pairs, 1,415 institutions never seen during training or validation:

Precision stayed extremely high throughout the model very rarely claims two different institutions are the same. Almost all of the error comes from the 21 false negatives: missed matches, not false alarms.

Accuracy holds at or above 97% for every country with a meaningful sample size. China, the largest single slice at 1,318 test pairs, comes in at 99.2%; no single region is propping up the global average.

The errors that remain all share one signature: near-zero lexical overlap between two strings naming the same place, a colloquial short form, or a sub-lab name with no textual relationship to its parent institution’s name. That’s a real-world-knowledge gap, not a training failure, and it’s the same category of error you’d expect from any system that has to infer identity from text alone.

Benchmarking against everything else I could get my hands on

A result in isolation doesn’t mean much, so I benchmarked the fine-tuned model against four other approaches, all on the exact same 129-pair held-out test set, with zero overlap with anything used in training:

  • A sentence-embedding cosine-similarity baseline (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) → a standard, widely-used DL approach to entity matching.
  • RapidFuzz token-sort-ratio → a strong classical string-similarity baseline, threshold-tuned on a held-out validation split.
  • ROR’s own affiliation-matching API → a real, production registry service used across the open-science ecosystem.
  • GPT-4o-mini, zero-shot, no fine-tuning, prompted directly to answer the same yes/no question. Total cost to benchmark: $0.0018, well under two-tenths of a cent.

A couple of things worth sitting with here.

GPT-4o-mini has perfect precision and the worst recall of anything tested. It’s extremely conservative; it only says “same” when the match is almost verbatim, and misses more than half of genuine matches that use different phrasing. That’s exactly the failure mode you’d predict for a general-purpose model asked to make a confident judgment on a domain it was never specifically trained for.

ROR and the fine-tuned model are the only two systems that hit anything close to perfect precision neither falsely merges two different institutions. But ROR misses far more real matches (72.1% recall) than the fine-tuned model (98.88–100% recall across the two evaluation sets). The classical and embedding baselines invert this entirely: they catch more matches, but with far more false alarms, because generic string or embedding similarity simply cannot distinguish “same institution, reworded” from “different institution, similarly named.”

That gap between generic similarity and an actual learned decision boundary for this specific task is what fine-tuning closes. And it closes it on free compute, in under an hour, with a model that runs inference in single-digit-to-low-double-digit milliseconds per decision, not the hundreds of milliseconds to seconds you’d pay for a hosted LLM call at scale.

How trustworthy is our training data, really?

Nobody has an official answer key for institution name disambiguation, so before trusting the resolver’s labels enough to fine-tune on, I checked them with claude to verify, on a random sample of 900 institutions, independent of the model entirely.

97.2% were correct. 21 were genuinely wrong, and 4 were too ambiguous for me to resolve confidently. Most of the real errors traced back to one specific, repeatable bug: when an institution’s name is generic or missing a distinguishing detail, the resolver occasionally grabs the wrong record from its catalog and the same wrong record gets reused across several unrelated real institutions.

The last two rows were the ones that actually mattered: I went back and checked whether this known error pattern had leaked into what the model was trained on. It had but barely. 3 contaminated pairs out of 17,500 training examples isn’t enough to meaningfully move a fine-tune of this size, and re-running the test evaluation with every affected label excluded changed the headline accuracy by exactly nothing (99.20% either way).

What this isn’t (yet)

In the interest of not overselling this:

  • The label source is ~97% accurate, not 100%. We measured this directly (above), rather than assuming it, but a 3% error rate in any label source is still a real ceiling on what “accuracy” against it can mean.
  • This is a pairwise verifier, not an end-to-end resolver. It answers “are these the same institution,” not “which of N institutions does this string match.” In a production pipeline, it sits downstream of a candidate-retrieval step, fuzzy match, or embedding search as a high-precision reranker, not a replacement for one.
  • Remaining errors cluster around real-world-knowledge gaps, colloquial names, sub-institutional naming with no lexical link to the parent, that no amount of more training data of the same kind will fully close. That likely needs either explicit knowledge injection or a retrieval component with access to institutional metadata beyond the raw string.
What’s next

Once the accompanying paper is ready and posted to arXiv, we will update it here. The training dataset itself will follow once we clear the compliance review currently blocking its release.

Github(Model Weights & Notebook) → https://github.com/Jeet009/institution-name-disambiguation-laya

If you work in scientometrics, bibliometrics, or research-integrity tooling and this is a problem you’ve also been quietly fighting with your own ad hoc string-matching rules: this won’t be the last word on institution name disambiguation, but for a weekend’s worth of free Kaggle GPU time, it’s a considerably better word than anything else I tried.

How I Fine-Tuned Laya to Solve an Important Problem in Scientometrics — With Claude Code was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR: Visualizing Patterns and Inconsistencies
items.summary: Why AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR Matter AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR transform how systematic literature reviews (SLRs) move from raw study lists to actionable evidence maps. In traditional workflows, reviewers manually code study characteristics, then struggle to spot cross-study patterns or conflicting findings. AI-native tagging applies structured labels at scale and surfaces those patterns and inconsistencies through interactive visualizations. This shift supports faster, more transparent evidence synthesis in healthcare and strengthens decision-making for HEOR, market access, and regulatory teams. The Challenge of Pattern Detection in Traditional SLR SLRs require exhaustive identification, screening, and synthesis of studies. Once data extraction is complete, analysts face a second bottleneck: turning hundreds of coded records into coherent insights . Manual tagging is slow, inconsistent across reviewers, and difficult to update when new evidence arrives. Patterns such as concentration of high-quality evidence in specific populations or repeated methodological gaps often remain buried in spreadsheets. Inconsistencies in outcome reporting, population definitions, or risk-of-bias assessments surface only after lengthy cross-checking. These limitations slow evidence synthesis in healthcare. Pharma and medical device teams preparing health technology assessments or value dossiers need clear visibility into where evidence is strong, weak, or conflicting. Without reliable visual tools, teams risk incomplete gap analysis, delayed submissions, or overlooked heterogeneity that affects later meta-analyses. What AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR Actually Are Three Capabilities. One Unified Evidence View. AI-Generated Tags An AI model reads each title, abstract, or full text and proposes tags that describe the article against the review’s PI(E)COS framework: population, intervention/exposure, comparator, outcomes, and study design. The tags are anchored to the passage that supports them, so a reviewer can open the article and see the highlighted sentence that justified “single-arm study” or “biologic-naive population.” Reviewers can accept, edit, or reject each tag. Tag Harmonization Raw AI tags are noisy in the same way human tags are. Harmonization is the step that fixes the vocabulary. Synonyms and near-duplicates are merged, and disease terms that refer to the same condition are mapped to one standard term. The harmonized set is then classified against the applicable inclusion and exclusion criteria. In AI tools for literature review , this standardization runs as part of tag generation rather than as a separate cleanup task, so the vocabulary is consistent from the first article. Tag Insights Once tags are harmonized and mapped to criteria, they can be visualized and cross-checked. Every article in title-and-abstract screening is included, with AI-generated and reviewer-added tags analyzed together, and a tag that appears more than once in one article counts once for that article. In practice, this produces a small family of views, each answering a different question about the corpus. Seven Ways to Understand an Evidence Corpus A well-structured evidence corpus can reveal more than which studies were included or excluded. Looking at the relationships between populations, interventions, comparators, outcomes, study designs, and other topics can uncover patterns, gaps, and inconsistencies that are difficult to see from individual articles alone. Seven Perspectives on the Evidence Understanding What the Evidence Contains A useful starting point is understanding the composition of the evidence. Examining how articles are distributed across PICOS criteria and other relevant topics shows which populations, interventions, outcomes, and study designs dominate the literature. It can also help answer focused questions, such as how much evidence exists for a particular population, treatment, or outcome combination. Tracing Evidence Across Criteria Looking at how criteria connect across articles provides another perspective. Common combinations reveal where evidence is concentrated, while uncommon or missing combinations can highlight areas where evidence is limited. This is particularly useful when assessing whether the available literature adequately supports specific protocol questions or subgroups. Identifying Common Tags and Evidence Gaps Tag frequency helps surface the most prevalent characteristics within the literature, while screening outcomes provide additional context on how those characteristics relate to relevance decisions. Coverage across criteria can also expose gaps. For example, limited comparator information may indicate that subsequent comparator-focused analysis will rely on an incomplete evidence base. Exploring Relationships Within the Evidence Examining how different criteria occur together can reveal patterns that simple frequency counts miss. Population and intervention combinations, for example, can show where research is concentrated and where evidence remains sparse. Adding study design or another dimension can further distinguish patterns across randomized, observational, or other types of evidence. Detecting Inconsistent Judgments Comparing independent signals of article relevance can help identify cases that deserve closer review. When relevance assessments and the characteristics captured from an article point in different directions, the disagreement may indicate ambiguity in the evidence or differences in how a criterion is being interpreted. These inconsistencies are not necessarily errors. They can serve as useful signals for quality review, helping researchers identify where evidence, criteria, or screening decisions may require additional scrutiny. How the Workflow Runs End to End The value of tag insights depends on where they sit in the review. The workflow below reflects how MadeAi implements it; other platforms will differ in labels but not in sequence. Two design choices keep this defensible. First, tags are generated per article and cost a fixed, visible amount, so teams can decide which subsets to tag rather than tagging everything by default. Second, every AI tag links to a passage in the source, which keeps the audit trail intact when the tag is later used as an exclusion reason. The same principle applies when AI reads figures rather than text, as described in Visual Data Extraction in SLRs: Can You Trust the Data?. Key Features That Separate Insights From Labels Benefits for Evidence Teams Faster reconciliation. When the Inconsistency Detector lists the articles where two judgments diverge, the reconciliation meeting starts with a short list instead of a full re-screen. Cleaner PRISMA reporting. Harmonized tags become countable exclusion reasons. The flow diagram and the excluded-studies appendix draw from the same source, which removes a common cause of mismatched numbers between the two. Earlier protocol feedback. If the Evidence Path shows that a single criterion is excluding most candidate articles, or Tag Verdict shows a tag that predicts exclusion far more than expected, the team can check whether the criterion is doing what the protocol intended before full-text screening begins. Visible coverage gaps. Completeness Radar makes missing information explicit. A criterion with low tag coverage is a known weakness in the evidence base rather than a surprise discovered during extraction. A defensible audit trail. Every tag that influences a decision links back to text in the article. That matters for regulatory submissions and for health technology assessment dossiers, where Market access solutions depend on evidence that can be traced to its source. Reusable structure. Tags generated once carry forward into later stages of the same review and into updates. For reviews that are refreshed on a schedule, this reduces the rework described in How AI and Living SLRs Can Power Dynamic JCA Evidence Mapping . Use Cases Oncology SLRs with dense comparator sets. Reviews of second-line and later therapies often exclude on comparator mismatch. Evidence Path makes the comparator criterion visible as a node, so the team can see how many candidate studies fell at that point and whether a broader comparator definition would change the picture. Rare disease reviews with small evidence bases. When the included set is under 30 studies, every borderline decision matters. The Inconsistency Detector gives a principled way to revisit each divergent article without re-screening the whole corpus. Clinical evaluation reports and PSURs. Device and pharmacovigilance reviews are repeated on fixed cycles. Harmonized tags let the next cycle start from a standard vocabulary rather than a fresh spreadsheet. This is the kind of repeatable work that AI-powered literature review services are built to support. Feasibility checks before meta-analysis. Before deciding whether a quantitative synthesis is possible, teams need to know how many studies share the same outcome definition and design. A Heatmap of Outcomes against Study Design, split by Comparator, answers that question from the screening data itself. For the distinction between the two exercises, see Systematic Literature Review vs Meta-Analysis . Global value dossiers. Pharma evidence generation solutions that feed HTA submissions need exclusion reasons that survive scrutiny. Tag-backed reasons with source highlights are easier to defend than reasons reconstructed months later. Best Practices for Adoption Fix the criteria before generating tags. Harmonization maps tags to criteria. If the criteria change mid-review, regenerate the tags for affected articles rather than editing them by hand. Tag the borderline set first. Tags cost credits per article. Start with articles marked “maybe” or with split reviewer decisions, where the insights change outcomes. Treat every flagged inconsistency as a question, not a verdict. Some disagreements reveal an ambiguous criterion. Others reveal an AI tag that misread a sentence. Record which it was. Confirm tags before they become exclusion reasons. Tag Highlights show the supporting sentence. Review it before the tag is used in the PRISMA appendix. Keep dual human screening where the protocol requires it. Tag insights add a third view of each article. They do not replace the second reviewer in protocols that mandate one. Read Completeness Radar before reading any other view. Every other chart is only as complete as tag coverage. Fix low-coverage criteria first, then interpret paths and heatmaps. Export the harmonized vocabulary with the review. The tag set is part of the methods. Store it alongside the search strategy. Limitations Tag insights are only as good as the tags beneath them, and AI tags carry known risks. Misread context. A model can tag “placebo-controlled” from a background sentence describing a different trial. Source highlights make this easy to catch, but only if someone looks. Harmonization overreach. Merging two disease terms that clinicians treat as distinct removes a real distinction. Review the merged pairs, particularly in rare disease and oncology subtypes. False confidence in agreement. When the title-and-abstract assessment and the tag-based assessment agree, both may still be wrong. Agreement reduces the reconciliation workload; it does not certify the decision. Cost at scale. Per-article tagging is affordable for a few hundred articles and needs budgeting for tens of thousands. Filter first, tag second. Model updates. Tags generated by different model versions may not be strictly comparable. Note the version used in the review’s methods, as you would for any screening tool. Reporting expectations. PRISMA 2020 asks authors to describe automation tools used in study selection. Tag generation and inconsistency detection fall within that scope and should be reported. None of these limits argue against the approach. They argue for using it inside a human-in-charge process, with the review team owning the final decisions. Where Tag Insights Are Heading Three developments are likely to shape the next generation of AI tools for systematic review . Living tag vocabularies. As reviews move to continuous update cycles, harmonized tags will be maintained across versions rather than regenerated each time, so that a new article can be placed on an existing Evidence Path without disturbing prior decisions. Cross-review pattern mining. Organizations that run many reviews in the same therapeutic area will be able to compare tag distributions across projects, revealing which criteria consistently exclude the most studies and where protocol language should be tightened. Deeper consistency checks. Today’s inconsistency detection compares two AI judgments about the same article. Future versions can compare human decisions against tag-implied decisions, and flag reviewers whose exclusion patterns diverge from the team’s, which turns a quality-control concern into a training signal. Each of these depends on the same foundation: tags that are consistent, source-linked, and mapped to criteria. That is the shift tag insights represent. Conclusion Screening tags have always contained more information than reviews used. AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR make that information visible by generating tags that link to their source, harmonizing them into a controlled vocabulary, and mapping them to the review’s criteria. The sunburst, frequency, and verdict views show what the corpus contains. Evidence Path and the Heatmap show how criteria combine. Completeness Radar shows what is missing, and the Inconsistency Detector shows where two views of an article disagree. Together they turn screening from a decision log into a dataset the team can examine while the review is still in progress. If your team is evaluating an AI platform for Life Sciences for evidence synthesis, ask to see the tags behind the decisions, not just the decisions. A Life Sciences solution that shows its tags, its harmonization rules, and its inconsistencies is one you can audit. That is the standard worth holding any AI-native tool to. AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR: Visualizing Patterns and Inconsistencies was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Why AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR Matter

AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR transform how systematic literature reviews (SLRs) move from raw study lists to actionable evidence maps. In traditional workflows, reviewers manually code study characteristics, then struggle to spot cross-study patterns or conflicting findings. AI-native tagging applies structured labels at scale and surfaces those patterns and inconsistencies through interactive visualizations. This shift supports faster, more transparent evidence synthesis in healthcare and strengthens decision-making for HEOR, market access, and regulatory teams.

The Challenge of Pattern Detection in Traditional SLR

SLRs require exhaustive identification, screening, and synthesis of studies. Once data extraction is complete, analysts face a second bottleneck: turning hundreds of coded records into coherent insights. Manual tagging is slow, inconsistent across reviewers, and difficult to update when new evidence arrives. Patterns such as concentration of high-quality evidence in specific populations or repeated methodological gaps often remain buried in spreadsheets. Inconsistencies in outcome reporting, population definitions, or risk-of-bias assessments surface only after lengthy cross-checking.

These limitations slow evidence synthesis in healthcare. Pharma and medical device teams preparing health technology assessments or value dossiers need clear visibility into where evidence is strong, weak, or conflicting. Without reliable visual tools, teams risk incomplete gap analysis, delayed submissions, or overlooked heterogeneity that affects later meta-analyses.

What AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR Actually AreThree Capabilities. One Unified Evidence View.AI-Generated Tags

An AI model reads each title, abstract, or full text and proposes tags that describe the article against the review’s PI(E)COS framework: population, intervention/exposure, comparator, outcomes, and study design. The tags are anchored to the passage that supports them, so a reviewer can open the article and see the highlighted sentence that justified “single-arm study” or “biologic-naive population.” Reviewers can accept, edit, or reject each tag.

Tag Harmonization

Raw AI tags are noisy in the same way human tags are. Harmonization is the step that fixes the vocabulary. Synonyms and near-duplicates are merged, and disease terms that refer to the same condition are mapped to one standard term. The harmonized set is then classified against the applicable inclusion and exclusion criteria. In AI tools for literature review, this standardization runs as part of tag generation rather than as a separate cleanup task, so the vocabulary is consistent from the first article.

Tag Insights

Once tags are harmonized and mapped to criteria, they can be visualized and cross-checked. Every article in title-and-abstract screening is included, with AI-generated and reviewer-added tags analyzed together, and a tag that appears more than once in one article counts once for that article. In practice, this produces a small family of views, each answering a different question about the corpus.

Seven Ways to Understand an Evidence Corpus

A well-structured evidence corpus can reveal more than which studies were included or excluded. Looking at the relationships between populations, interventions, comparators, outcomes, study designs, and other topics can uncover patterns, gaps, and inconsistencies that are difficult to see from individual articles alone.

Seven Perspectives on the EvidenceUnderstanding What the Evidence Contains

A useful starting point is understanding the composition of the evidence. Examining how articles are distributed across PICOS criteria and other relevant topics shows which populations, interventions, outcomes, and study designs dominate the literature. It can also help answer focused questions, such as how much evidence exists for a particular population, treatment, or outcome combination.

Tracing Evidence Across Criteria

Looking at how criteria connect across articles provides another perspective. Common combinations reveal where evidence is concentrated, while uncommon or missing combinations can highlight areas where evidence is limited. This is particularly useful when assessing whether the available literature adequately supports specific protocol questions or subgroups.

Identifying Common Tags and Evidence Gaps

Tag frequency helps surface the most prevalent characteristics within the literature, while screening outcomes provide additional context on how those characteristics relate to relevance decisions. Coverage across criteria can also expose gaps. For example, limited comparator information may indicate that subsequent comparator-focused analysis will rely on an incomplete evidence base.

Exploring Relationships Within the Evidence

Examining how different criteria occur together can reveal patterns that simple frequency counts miss. Population and intervention combinations, for example, can show where research is concentrated and where evidence remains sparse. Adding study design or another dimension can further distinguish patterns across randomized, observational, or other types of evidence.

Detecting Inconsistent Judgments

Comparing independent signals of article relevance can help identify cases that deserve closer review. When relevance assessments and the characteristics captured from an article point in different directions, the disagreement may indicate ambiguity in the evidence or differences in how a criterion is being interpreted.

These inconsistencies are not necessarily errors. They can serve as useful signals for quality review, helping researchers identify where evidence, criteria, or screening decisions may require additional scrutiny.

How the Workflow Runs End to End

The value of tag insights depends on where they sit in the review. The workflow below reflects how MadeAi implements it; other platforms will differ in labels but not in sequence.

Two design choices keep this defensible. First, tags are generated per article and cost a fixed, visible amount, so teams can decide which subsets to tag rather than tagging everything by default. Second, every AI tag links to a passage in the source, which keeps the audit trail intact when the tag is later used as an exclusion reason. The same principle applies when AI reads figures rather than text, as described in Visual Data Extraction in SLRs: Can You Trust the Data?.

Key Features That Separate Insights From LabelsBenefits for Evidence Teams

Faster reconciliation. When the Inconsistency Detector lists the articles where two judgments diverge, the reconciliation meeting starts with a short list instead of a full re-screen.

Cleaner PRISMA reporting. Harmonized tags become countable exclusion reasons. The flow diagram and the excluded-studies appendix draw from the same source, which removes a common cause of mismatched numbers between the two.

Earlier protocol feedback. If the Evidence Path shows that a single criterion is excluding most candidate articles, or Tag Verdict shows a tag that predicts exclusion far more than expected, the team can check whether the criterion is doing what the protocol intended before full-text screening begins.

Visible coverage gaps. Completeness Radar makes missing information explicit. A criterion with low tag coverage is a known weakness in the evidence base rather than a surprise discovered during extraction.

A defensible audit trail. Every tag that influences a decision links back to text in the article. That matters for regulatory submissions and for health technology assessment dossiers, where Market access solutions depend on evidence that can be traced to its source.

Reusable structure. Tags generated once carry forward into later stages of the same review and into updates. For reviews that are refreshed on a schedule, this reduces the rework described in How AI and Living SLRs Can Power Dynamic JCA Evidence Mapping.

Use Cases

Oncology SLRs with dense comparator sets. Reviews of second-line and later therapies often exclude on comparator mismatch. Evidence Path makes the comparator criterion visible as a node, so the team can see how many candidate studies fell at that point and whether a broader comparator definition would change the picture.

Rare disease reviews with small evidence bases. When the included set is under 30 studies, every borderline decision matters. The Inconsistency Detector gives a principled way to revisit each divergent article without re-screening the whole corpus.

Clinical evaluation reports and PSURs. Device and pharmacovigilance reviews are repeated on fixed cycles. Harmonized tags let the next cycle start from a standard vocabulary rather than a fresh spreadsheet. This is the kind of repeatable work that AI-powered literature review services are built to support.

Feasibility checks before meta-analysis. Before deciding whether a quantitative synthesis is possible, teams need to know how many studies share the same outcome definition and design. A Heatmap of Outcomes against Study Design, split by Comparator, answers that question from the screening data itself. For the distinction between the two exercises, see Systematic Literature Review vs Meta-Analysis.

Global value dossiers. Pharma evidence generation solutions that feed HTA submissions need exclusion reasons that survive scrutiny. Tag-backed reasons with source highlights are easier to defend than reasons reconstructed months later.

Best Practices for Adoption
  1. Fix the criteria before generating tags. Harmonization maps tags to criteria. If the criteria change mid-review, regenerate the tags for affected articles rather than editing them by hand.
  2. Tag the borderline set first. Tags cost credits per article. Start with articles marked “maybe” or with split reviewer decisions, where the insights change outcomes.
  3. Treat every flagged inconsistency as a question, not a verdict. Some disagreements reveal an ambiguous criterion. Others reveal an AI tag that misread a sentence. Record which it was.
  4. Confirm tags before they become exclusion reasons. Tag Highlights show the supporting sentence. Review it before the tag is used in the PRISMA appendix.
  5. Keep dual human screening where the protocol requires it. Tag insights add a third view of each article. They do not replace the second reviewer in protocols that mandate one.
  6. Read Completeness Radar before reading any other view. Every other chart is only as complete as tag coverage. Fix low-coverage criteria first, then interpret paths and heatmaps.
  7. Export the harmonized vocabulary with the review. The tag set is part of the methods. Store it alongside the search strategy.
Limitations

Tag insights are only as good as the tags beneath them, and AI tags carry known risks.

  • Misread context. A model can tag “placebo-controlled” from a background sentence describing a different trial. Source highlights make this easy to catch, but only if someone looks.
  • Harmonization overreach. Merging two disease terms that clinicians treat as distinct removes a real distinction. Review the merged pairs, particularly in rare disease and oncology subtypes.
  • False confidence in agreement. When the title-and-abstract assessment and the tag-based assessment agree, both may still be wrong. Agreement reduces the reconciliation workload; it does not certify the decision.
  • Cost at scale. Per-article tagging is affordable for a few hundred articles and needs budgeting for tens of thousands. Filter first, tag second.
  • Model updates. Tags generated by different model versions may not be strictly comparable. Note the version used in the review’s methods, as you would for any screening tool.
  • Reporting expectations. PRISMA 2020 asks authors to describe automation tools used in study selection. Tag generation and inconsistency detection fall within that scope and should be reported.

None of these limits argue against the approach. They argue for using it inside a human-in-charge process, with the review team owning the final decisions.

Where Tag Insights Are Heading

Three developments are likely to shape the next generation of AI tools for systematic review.

Living tag vocabularies. As reviews move to continuous update cycles, harmonized tags will be maintained across versions rather than regenerated each time, so that a new article can be placed on an existing Evidence Path without disturbing prior decisions.

Cross-review pattern mining. Organizations that run many reviews in the same therapeutic area will be able to compare tag distributions across projects, revealing which criteria consistently exclude the most studies and where protocol language should be tightened.

Deeper consistency checks. Today’s inconsistency detection compares two AI judgments about the same article. Future versions can compare human decisions against tag-implied decisions, and flag reviewers whose exclusion patterns diverge from the team’s, which turns a quality-control concern into a training signal.

Each of these depends on the same foundation: tags that are consistent, source-linked, and mapped to criteria. That is the shift tag insights represent.

Conclusion

Screening tags have always contained more information than reviews used. AI-Native Tag Insights in SLR make that information visible by generating tags that link to their source, harmonizing them into a controlled vocabulary, and mapping them to the review’s criteria. The sunburst, frequency, and verdict views show what the corpus contains. Evidence Path and the Heatmap show how criteria combine. Completeness Radar shows what is missing, and the Inconsistency Detector shows where two views of an article disagree. Together they turn screening from a decision log into a dataset the team can examine while the review is still in progress.

If your team is evaluating an AI platform for Life Sciences for evidence synthesis, ask to see the tags behind the decisions, not just the decisions. A Life Sciences solution that shows its tags, its harmonization rules, and its inconsistencies is one you can audit. That is the standard worth holding any AI-native tool to.

Work, he wrote, for the elimination of concrete evils rather than for the realization of abstract goods.
