Complexity: a reservoir hidden among up to 1,000 loud but irrelevant town facts. Interconnectedness: a plan to close a weir, and a shuffled rulebook of up to eleven steps from the weir to the school bus that cannot run. Dynamics: six weeks of algae readings, and whether algae will cover half the lake by week twenty. Intransparency: a paper mill accused on a lab test, or only on a proxy, a cue, its own statement or a rumour. Many goals: a council’s list of 3 to 32 goals, with or without a hidden contradiction. Novelty: the same flood chain in familiar words, invented words, and rules that contradict what everyone knows. Figure 1 shows how much probability Jev put on the right answer in each case. Four of the six features did not touch it: the reservoir was found among a thousand facts as surely as among none, the school bus eleven steps away, the mill’s guilt left open with “cannot tell” when the evidence was a proxy or a rumour, invented words read as written. On 42 of the 44 cases it was right. The two that broke it, Schaub would have predicted, with a twist. Given raw weekly numbers, Jev could barely tell a lake that would be half covered from one that would not, and judged a series growing 25% a week wrong, at 0.47: the failure Schaub reports for people. The goal lists broke it the other way round. Dörner’s mayors did not notice contradictions between their goals; Jev, asked whether two goals contradict each other when none did, put the probability at 0.21 with three goals and 0.57 with thirty-two. People miss conflicts; the critic drifted toward inventing them. Figure 1 — The critic under test: 44 cases, six features, harsher levels left to right. Image by the author. 4. A critic must know when it does not know. Here the critic parted company with Dörner’s mayors, who went wrong with conviction. Jev’s confidence, averaged over the 44 cases, was 0.86 when it was right and 0.55 when it was wrong (figure 2). Draw a line at 0.7 and let code act only above it, and code acts on 38 cases without a single error and hands six to a person , exactly where it had failed: four growth series and the two longest goal lists without a conflict. This is C. K. Chow’s rule of 1970 for a classifier that may abstain; read backwards, a floor at 0.7 says a referral costs about 30% of a wrong answer. It is optimal only when the probabilities are honest, as Hendrickx and colleagues’ 2021 survey notes, and section 6 is where they stop being. Figure 2 — Every answer by its confidence: the two errors sit below the 0.7 floor. Image by the author. 5. The critic’s evidence must be prepared, and the preparer criticized. Schaub’s remedies for people, forecast, build a model of the system, break the goals into parts, and the vendor’s advice to keep the arithmetic in code and send only what the question needs are the same list, and Popper’s too: no criticism without a stated claim and prepared evidence. So each remedy became a few lines of code run before Jev reads anything. Given the growth rate in words (“it doubles about every 3.1 weeks”), the critic did better, 0.71 on the series that had failed; given a projection computed by code (“passes 50% in week 19”), it answered between 0.95 and 0.97 on the series that pass and 0.02 on the ones that do not (figure 3). Code that chained the declared rules in causal order moved the eleven-step case from 0.72 to 0.94. The critic does not need to be taught growth. It needs the growth done. My first version of the chaining code kept one effect per cause, so a side branch overwrote the main chain and Jev answered 0.07 and 0.03 on two cases whose right answer was yes. That is central reduction from Schaub’s catalogue, a networked system treated as one line of causes, committed by the person who prepares the critic’s evidence and caught only because the lab knew the answers. The critic’s input is a conjecture too. Figure 3 — Growth: the critic needs the arithmetic done, not described. Image by the author. 6. Popper’s question, asked of every reason. What can a critic that cannot plan check in a policymaker’s reason? Not whether it is true; the world decides that. Whether it is the kind of claim the world could decide. So I asked Jev Popper’s question of every reason the experiment had produced: how could the coming months show this reason to have been wrong? Scored on three levels: nothing in it could be shown wrong; it expects an outcome but names no measure, place or time to check it; it names what it expects to see, where and by when. Code counted a reason testable when Jev put the top level at even odds or better. The reasons were the 34 I had planted earlier to test the critic on Schaub’s catalogue of errors (four for each of six errors, four clean ones, six near misses that look like an error and are not), the 24 an AI mayor gave while governing a lake town for a year, twice, which section 7 describes, and 10 fresh samples of one month of that year. Figure 4 shows what Popper’s question separates and what it does not. Immunization was never testable, 0 of 4, which is its definition. Methodism, repeating what worked before without checking the conditions, 0 of 4. Momentary extrapolation, the current trend drawn straight forward, 4 of 4: a bold conjecture the data could refute, which Dörner lists as an error because his mayors did not revise it when the data did. Wishful thinking and the clean reasons each split 2 of 4: “it will be fine by summer” is a prediction summer can refute, however badly argued, and a sound reason to wait and look is not yet a prediction. And the near misses, 3 of 6, included sentences as testable as any in the set, among them the compounding sentence, “if that compounding continues it doubles every three weeks, so I’ll act now”. Testability is not truth, and it is not soundness. It is the admission ticket to criticism. Figure 4 — Popper’s question to every reason: could the coming months show it wrong? Image by the author. That is where Dörner’s psychology and Popper’s logic part, and the critic sided with the psychology. The two sentences the critic had earlier flagged as errors, wrongly, are among the three near misses Popper’s question passed (figure 5): the beach reason as methodism at 0.88, although it checks exactly the condition that defines methodism, and the compounding sentence as momentary extrapolation at 0.95. The critic had caught all twenty-four planted errors, most at 0.93 or higher, and was fooled by sentences that wear the surface of an error while doing what Popper asks for. No confidence floor catches a mistake at 0.95. A second, literal yes-or-no question about whether the reason checks a present fact, combined in code, left one miss in thirty-four, written after seeing the misses. The mayor answered Popper’s question more bleakly: 5 of its 24 reasons named what would show them wrong , 3 of 12 without a coach and 2 of 12 with one. The coach’s note, which only ever spoke about side effects, left that unchanged in the month sampled five times each way: 1 of 5 reasons testable without the note, 2 of 5 with it. An AI policymaker, left to itself, mostly does not say what would prove it wrong, and a coach that criticizes reasons did not teach it to. Figure 5 — Planted errors, clean reasons, near misses: both misses were confident. Image by the author. 7. Refuting a reason is not refuting a policy. Then Jev got the trainer’s job. The town is a Lohhausen of my own, declared in a few dozen lines of code: algae the quiet critical variable, compounding at 35% a month, harming tourism above 15% of the lake, responding to a cut in farm phosphate only from the third month after the order; tourism the loud one, dipping every off-season, recovering by itself, making the headline whenever it is low; dredging halving the algae at once but making it grow faster for two months. Waiting or chasing headlines ends with algae over 73% of the lake; two early cuts end at 10%. The mayor was DeepSeek’s flash model, choosing one action a month with a sentence of reason. Jev read every reason, with the town in words rather than numbers, and answered three questions: which catalogue error, if any; does it check the conditions; does it mention a delayed effect or a side effect of the chosen action. The coach spoke on a confident error or a reason blind to side effects, and only ever named the error, never what to do. The year ran twice, with the notes passed on and with the coach silent. In month 2 the mayor dredged, with a reason that spoke of immediate results and said nothing about delayed or side effects; Jev put that at 0.21, and the coach said so. It was the most useful note of the year: that side effect adds ten points to the 45% by which the algae grow in month 3. In month 3 the mayor promoted tourism in both runs; the coached reason now mentioned the slow phosphate effect. One month is one sample, so I asked month 3 again, five times with the note and five without (figure 6). Without the note, two of five reasons named a delayed or side effect; with it, five of five. The action did not move. Promote tourism, ten times out of ten. Popper has a name for what the coached mayor did: its reasons improved and its deed stayed, the claim repaired until the criticism no longer touched it, the immunizing move performed by a language model prompted to reflect. What this is not is Goodhart’s law. The mayor was not gaming anyone; the note only ever talked about words. What did not happen is the step a critic exists for, from seeing the flaw in a reason to reconsidering the decision. And then the world did what the critic could not. The coached mayor’s month-3 reason forecast that “the earlier phosphate cut should keep reducing algae slowly”. Month 4 refuted it: the algae stood at 2.8% of the lake, up from 2.0, the cut not yet acting, and the mayor said so in its next reason, “rising despite early phosphate cuts”, and dredged. That was the year’s one refutation, and the critic never saw it . Reading one reason at a time, it scored the month-4 reason as momentary extrapolation at 0.57 and moved on. A critic that reads sentences cannot compare results expected with results achieved; only code holding last month’s claim against this month’s lake can, the piecemeal engineer’s whole job, and nothing in the loop did it. Two cautions. Three of the five coached reasons named only the earlier cut’s delay, not the campaign’s, and Jev, asked about the chosen action, scored them 0.69 to 0.94 anyway. And whether the action should have changed, nothing here can say: my code labelled it repair-service behaviour, but the growth was from 2.0% to 2.8% of the lake, far below the harm line, and both years ended with a clean lake, at 2.1% and 2.6%. The label is a definition, not a verdict , and a deed could be labelled at all only because the town was declared with its critical variable named. The two runs drifted apart from month 5 on; with one run each way that cannot be told from noise. Figure 6 — Month 3, five fresh samples each: the note moved the reasons, not the decision. Image by the author. 8. Who checks the checker. What an AI critic needs from a policy process follows from where this one worked and where it went blind. Claims stated so that they can fail: Popper’s question as an intake filter, and the mayor’s 5 of 24 says how much of what passes for a reason would survive it. Effects named in advance and compared by code when they arrive , because the critic cannot do that part and the one refutation of the year went unseen. Steps small enough to disentangle cause from effect , Popper’s condition for learning at all; the declared town is the extreme case. A floor below which a person decides , knowing it does not catch confident mistakes. And Donald Campbell’s warning: an indicator used for social decisions comes under pressure to be corrupted and distorts what it was meant to monitor. A critic’s score on reasons, used at scale, would be such an indicator. The last requirement is Popper’s own, turned on the instrument. His institutions exist so that rulers can be removed without bloodshed; a checker nobody can appeal is a ruler, and the two near misses flagged at 0.95 and 0.88 had no appeal. The answer is not a better checker but the open society’s: the critic’s answers recorded and public, so that anyone can show where it was wrong; planted controls with known answers, run on every version, as the critic’s own trial; a person above the floor and one who reads the appeals. The numbers are small: 44 lab cases, 68 reasons, one year each way and one month sampled five times each way, one town, one critic version, which its vendor expects to improve, one mayor model. The reasons were written to order by a language model, the second condition question after I had seen the misses. These are demonstrations, a model of the argument and not evidence about ministries. A machine can tell you whether a policy claim could be wrong. Only the world can tell you whether it is. Popper’s advice was to work for the elimination of concrete evils rather than for the realization of abstract goods. A critic that cannot plan can help with that. Refutation still needs a world small enough to answer, and someone who checks the checker. Sources: K. R. Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), vol. 1, ch. 7; The Poverty of Historicism (1957), §21; Conjectures and Refutations (1963), ch. 1 and ch. 16, pp. 361 and 385; Objektive Erkenntnis (1973), p. 43, on Hans Albert’s term; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Popper; H. Schaub, “Störungen und Fehler beim Denken und Problemlösen”, in J. Funke (ed.), Denken und Problemlösen, Hogrefe 2006, pp. 447–482; D. Dörner et al., Lohhausen (1983); the University of Bamberg’s Dörner page; TypeSafe, “System One”, and “Jev 1.13 jaggedness” (that page reviewed 2026–10–02); L. Zheng et al., “Judging LLM-as-a-Judge”, NeurIPS 2023; C. K. Chow, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 16 (1970), 41–46; K. Hendrickx et al., “Machine Learning with a Reject Option” (2021); D. T. Campbell, Evaluation and Program Planning 2 (1979). The Critic Who Cannot Plan was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

It is optimal only when the probabilities are honest, as Hendrickx and colleagues’ 2021 survey notes, and section 6 is where they stop being.

Figure 2 — Every answer by its confidence: the two errors sit below the 0.7 floor. Image by the author.5. The critic’s evidence must be prepared, and the preparer criticized.

Schaub’s remedies for people, forecast, build a model of the system, break the goals into parts, and the vendor’s advice to keep the arithmetic in code and send only what the question needs are the same list, and Popper’s too: no criticism without a stated claim and prepared evidence. So each remedy became a few lines of code run before Jev reads anything. Given the growth rate in words (“it doubles about every 3.1 weeks”), the critic did better, 0.71 on the series that had failed; given a projection computed by code (“passes 50% in week 19”), it answered between 0.95 and 0.97 on the series that pass and 0.02 on the ones that do not (figure 3). Code that chained the declared rules in causal order moved the eleven-step case from 0.72 to 0.94. The critic does not need to be taught growth. It needs the growth done.

My first version of the chaining code kept one effect per cause, so a side branch overwrote the main chain and Jev answered 0.07 and 0.03 on two cases whose right answer was yes. That is central reduction from Schaub’s catalogue, a networked system treated as one line of causes, committed by the person who prepares the critic’s evidence and caught only because the lab knew the answers. The critic’s input is a conjecture too.

Figure 3 — Growth: the critic needs the arithmetic done, not described. Image by the author.6. Popper’s question, asked of every reason.

What can a critic that cannot plan check in a policymaker’s reason? Not whether it is true; the world decides that. Whether it is the kind of claim the world could decide. So I asked Jev Popper’s question of every reason the experiment had produced: how could the coming months show this reason to have been wrong? Scored on three levels: nothing in it could be shown wrong; it expects an outcome but names no measure, place or time to check it; it names what it expects to see, where and by when. Code counted a reason testable when Jev put the top level at even odds or better.

The reasons were the 34 I had planted earlier to test the critic on Schaub’s catalogue of errors (four for each of six errors, four clean ones, six near misses that look like an error and are not), the 24 an AI mayor gave while governing a lake town for a year, twice, which section 7 describes, and 10 fresh samples of one month of that year.

Figure 4 shows what Popper’s question separates and what it does not. Immunization was never testable, 0 of 4, which is its definition. Methodism, repeating what worked before without checking the conditions, 0 of 4. Momentary extrapolation, the current trend drawn straight forward, 4 of 4: a bold conjecture the data could refute, which Dörner lists as an error because his mayors did not revise it when the data did. Wishful thinking and the clean reasons each split 2 of 4: “it will be fine by summer” is a prediction summer can refute, however badly argued, and a sound reason to wait and look is not yet a prediction. And the near misses, 3 of 6, included sentences as testable as any in the set, among them the compounding sentence, “if that compounding continues it doubles every three weeks, so I’ll act now”. Testability is not truth, and it is not soundness. It is the admission ticket to criticism.

Figure 4 — Popper’s question to every reason: could the coming months show it wrong? Image by the author.

That is where Dörner’s psychology and Popper’s logic part, and the critic sided with the psychology. The two sentences the critic had earlier flagged as errors, wrongly, are among the three near misses Popper’s question passed (figure 5): the beach reason as methodism at 0.88, although it checks exactly the condition that defines methodism, and the compounding sentence as momentary extrapolation at 0.95. The critic had caught all twenty-four planted errors, most at 0.93 or higher, and was fooled by sentences that wear the surface of an error while doing what Popper asks for. No confidence floor catches a mistake at 0.95. A second, literal yes-or-no question about whether the reason checks a present fact, combined in code, left one miss in thirty-four, written after seeing the misses.

The mayor answered Popper’s question more bleakly: 5 of its 24 reasons named what would show them wrong, 3 of 12 without a coach and 2 of 12 with one. The coach’s note, which only ever spoke about side effects, left that unchanged in the month sampled five times each way: 1 of 5 reasons testable without the note, 2 of 5 with it. An AI policymaker, left to itself, mostly does not say what would prove it wrong, and a coach that criticizes reasons did not teach it to.

Figure 5 — Planted errors, clean reasons, near misses: both misses were confident. Image by the author.7. Refuting a reason is not refuting a policy.

Then Jev got the trainer’s job. The town is a Lohhausen of my own, declared in a few dozen lines of code: algae the quiet critical variable, compounding at 35% a month, harming tourism above 15% of the lake, responding to a cut in farm phosphate only from the third month after the order; tourism the loud one, dipping every off-season, recovering by itself, making the headline whenever it is low; dredging halving the algae at once but making it grow faster for two months. Waiting or chasing headlines ends with algae over 73% of the lake; two early cuts end at 10%. The mayor was DeepSeek’s flash model, choosing one action a month with a sentence of reason. Jev read every reason, with the town in words rather than numbers, and answered three questions: which catalogue error, if any; does it check the conditions; does it mention a delayed effect or a side effect of the chosen action. The coach spoke on a confident error or a reason blind to side effects, and only ever named the error, never what to do. The year ran twice, with the notes passed on and with the coach silent.

In month 2 the mayor dredged, with a reason that spoke of immediate results and said nothing about delayed or side effects; Jev put that at 0.21, and the coach said so. It was the most useful note of the year: that side effect adds ten points to the 45% by which the algae grow in month 3. In month 3 the mayor promoted tourism in both runs; the coached reason now mentioned the slow phosphate effect. One month is one sample, so I asked month 3 again, five times with the note and five without (figure 6). Without the note, two of five reasons named a delayed or side effect; with it, five of five. The action did not move. Promote tourism, ten times out of ten.

Popper has a name for what the coached mayor did: its reasons improved and its deed stayed, the claim repaired until the criticism no longer touched it, the immunizing move performed by a language model prompted to reflect. What this is not is Goodhart’s law. The mayor was not gaming anyone; the note only ever talked about words. What did not happen is the step a critic exists for, from seeing the flaw in a reason to reconsidering the decision.

And then the world did what the critic could not. The coached mayor’s month-3 reason forecast that “the earlier phosphate cut should keep reducing algae slowly”. Month 4 refuted it: the algae stood at 2.8% of the lake, up from 2.0, the cut not yet acting, and the mayor said so in its next reason, “rising despite early phosphate cuts”, and dredged. That was the year’s one refutation, and the critic never saw it. Reading one reason at a time, it scored the month-4 reason as momentary extrapolation at 0.57 and moved on. A critic that reads sentences cannot compare results expected with results achieved; only code holding last month’s claim against this month’s lake can, the piecemeal engineer’s whole job, and nothing in the loop did it.

Two cautions. Three of the five coached reasons named only the earlier cut’s delay, not the campaign’s, and Jev, asked about the chosen action, scored them 0.69 to 0.94 anyway. And whether the action should have changed, nothing here can say: my code labelled it repair-service behaviour, but the growth was from 2.0% to 2.8% of the lake, far below the harm line, and both years ended with a clean lake, at 2.1% and 2.6%. The label is a definition, not a verdict, and a deed could be labelled at all only because the town was declared with its critical variable named. The two runs drifted apart from month 5 on; with one run each way that cannot be told from noise.

Figure 6 — Month 3, five fresh samples each: the note moved the reasons, not the decision. Image by the author.8. Who checks the checker.

What an AI critic needs from a policy process follows from where this one worked and where it went blind. Claims stated so that they can fail: Popper’s question as an intake filter, and the mayor’s 5 of 24 says how much of what passes for a reason would survive it. Effects named in advance and compared by code when they arrive, because the critic cannot do that part and the one refutation of the year went unseen. Steps small enough to disentangle cause from effect, Popper’s condition for learning at all; the declared town is the extreme case. A floor below which a person decides, knowing it does not catch confident mistakes. And Donald Campbell’s warning: an indicator used for social decisions comes under pressure to be corrupted and distorts what it was meant to monitor. A critic’s score on reasons, used at scale, would be such an indicator.

The last requirement is Popper’s own, turned on the instrument. His institutions exist so that rulers can be removed without bloodshed; a checker nobody can appeal is a ruler, and the two near misses flagged at 0.95 and 0.88 had no appeal. The answer is not a better checker but the open society’s: the critic’s answers recorded and public, so that anyone can show where it was wrong; planted controls with known answers, run on every version, as the critic’s own trial; a person above the floor and one who reads the appeals.

The numbers are small: 44 lab cases, 68 reasons, one year each way and one month sampled five times each way, one town, one critic version, which its vendor expects to improve, one mayor model. The reasons were written to order by a language model, the second condition question after I had seen the misses. These are demonstrations, a model of the argument and not evidence about ministries.

A machine can tell you whether a policy claim could be wrong. Only the world can tell you whether it is. Popper’s advice was to work for the elimination of concrete evils rather than for the realization of abstract goods. A critic that cannot plan can help with that. Refutation still needs a world small enough to answer, and someone who checks the checker.

Sources: K. R. Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), vol. 1, ch. 7; The Poverty of Historicism (1957), §21; Conjectures and Refutations (1963), ch. 1 and ch. 16, pp. 361 and 385; Objektive Erkenntnis (1973), p. 43, on Hans Albert’s term; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Popper; H. Schaub, “Störungen und Fehler beim Denken und Problemlösen”, in J. Funke (ed.), Denken und Problemlösen, Hogrefe 2006, pp. 447–482; D. Dörner et al., Lohhausen (1983); the University of Bamberg’s Dörner page; TypeSafe, “System One”, and “Jev 1.13 jaggedness” (that page reviewed 2026–10–02); L. Zheng et al., “Judging LLM-as-a-Judge”, NeurIPS 2023; C. K. Chow, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 16 (1970), 41–46; K. Hendrickx et al., “Machine Learning with a Reject Option” (2021); D. T. Campbell, Evaluation and Program Planning 2 (1979).

items.title: What Is Jev? What the Tests Show and Who Should Try It
items.summary: A new model called Jev is built for this kind of job. You give it the ticket and the possible answers, and it returns a choice with a probability, nothing else. A startup called TypeSafe AI released it on September 15. The company says a response takes 70 to 500 milliseconds, and a million input tokens cost $0.042. Output tokens are free. A note on how this article was made: I used Claude to help read the documentation, the announcement post and the independent tests, and to draft the text. All numbers come from the sources linked at the end. My own experience is in a separate section, “My experience”. The same ticket, two ways to answer it. What it is A regular LLM writes its answer one word at a time. Jev cannot do that. It reads a situation and a few questions, and returns numbers. Think of a security guard at the door. The guard does not write a report. The guard decides in a second: let the person in, turn them away, or call a supervisor. Jev works the same way. There are three kinds of questions: Choice: pick one option from a list, for example which team should handle a ticket. Score: rate something on a scale you describe, for example how frustrated a customer is. Noul: a yes or no question, for example whether a message is urgent. Every answer comes with a probability. When the model is unsure, you can see it and send the case to a person or to a stronger model. How it works Here is an example from the documentation. A customer writes: “I’ve been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and the integration keeps failing. I’m losing sales. Please help ASAP.” You ask which team should handle it and whether it is urgent: from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, TypeSafeClient client = TypeSafeClient() # reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY from the environment ticket = "Hi, I've been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and the integration keeps failing. I'm losing sales. Please help ASAP." response = client.system_one( state=ticket, questions={ "department": Choice( instructions="Which team should handle this", criteria={ "billing": "Payment or subscription issues", "technical": "Bugs or integration problems", "sales": "Pricing or account questions", }, ), "is_urgent": Noul( instructions="The message conveys urgency or time-sensitivity", ), }, ) print(response.answers["department"].choice) # "technical" print(response.answers["is_urgent"].noul) # 1.0 In the documentation’s example the answer is technical with 85% probability, billing 15%, sales 0%, and urgent: yes. All questions go out in one request and are evaluated in parallel. That is where the speed comes from: the model does not write a long answer word by word. The company calls output tokens “too cheap to meter”, so they are free. For Choice and Score answers you also get a confidence number from 0 to 1. You pick the threshold. In the documentation’s example, anything below 0.5 goes to a person. A few things to know before your first request: Input is text only. No images or audio. There is one model for everyone. You cannot fine-tune it on your data, so you shape it with the wording of your questions. The answer options must be defined in advance: a list, a scale or yes/no. The name jev-latest points to the current version and changes with releases. If you tuned thresholds, pin the version number (it is 1.13.0 now). What the tests show It comes from the company’s own tests. If you recompute it from their table, 444.6 is the price of the most expensive model there (Opus 5) divided by the price of Jev. The authors themselves call these numbers the high end of real gains. Against small models the gain is smaller. In independent tests Jev was about 4 to 27 times cheaper and 2.6 to 23 times faster. That is still a lot. Sources: evals.typesafe.ai, MLflow, Braintrust, jev-phishing-bench. Multiples marked ~ are approximate or calculated by the author from published figures. Accuracy is the harder question, and there are only a few independent tests: A phishing test on 2,000 synthetic on emails — on one general question, “is this phishing?”, Jev lost: 62.6% against 81.3% for Claude Haiku 4.5. Then the author split the task into five simple questions and combined the answers with a simple formula. Jev reached 95.0% and Haiku 93.2%, a tie on accuracy, but Jev was 27 times cheaper and 5 times faster. The author notes that the emails are synthetic and that the questions were written after studying the dataset. MLflow (Databricks) — as a judge on 30 hand-labeled examples, Jev agreed with humans 30 times out of 30, like GPT-5.6 Terra and Luna. The median latency was 369 ms, and it cost $0.0247 per thousand judgments against $0.06 to $3.78 for the others. The sample is small, and the authors advise testing on your own data. Braintrust — on checking whether a claim is supported by a source, Jev scored best at 80.2%, but the next model was at 79.2%, which is within noise. On judging whether an answer is correct it was weaker: 78.1% against 88.6% for Luna with reasoning, and 19 to 20 points behind on math and code. Classmethod — an engineer tested Jev as the classifier of an LLM router with four difficulty levels, calling the API directly and not plugging it into the router. In 40 requests it picked the right level every time, at about 0.65 seconds per request. The classifiers in the original article took 2.1 and 7.2 seconds. The author does not call this a benchmark. Jev does not replace a strong model. It answers simple questions fast and cheaply, especially when you split a complex decision into several simple ones. What people say David Linthicum , an independent consultant, told InfoWorld that many companies use a large LLM as a universal layer, even when the application only needs a quick choice from a few options. He sees Jev next to regular models: Jev for frequent simple decisions, the big model for reasoning and text. Stephanie Walter of HyperFrame Research says developers will have to define questions, possible answers, thresholds and escalation paths in advance, which can be a lot of work, and that accuracy and calibration must be checked on your own data. Paul Chada of Doozer AI points out that a probability shows how confident the model is, but not why. In regulated industries that is an audit problem. Advait Patel of Broadcom says the approach could make control flow more explicit and easier to test, because the logic moves from prompts back into code. He also lists the risks of an early-stage vendor: security, data location, availability guarantees and dependency. The service currently runs in a single region. The Register called the “zero hallucinations” claim an unfair comparison, because Jev does not write text and a structured answer can still be wrong. Every reports that OpenAI previewed a Decisions API in late September with the same idea (context plus a fixed set of answers) and image input. The price is not announced. In Every’s informal tests, Decisions picked the right interface control in 76 of 78 steps against 73 for Jev. On classifying conversations, accuracy was about equal and Jev was faster: 161 ms against 309 ms. Where it fits and who should try it Where it fits: Routing: where to send a customer request, or which model should handle a query. This is the case the Classmethod engineer tested. First-line checks: guardrails for LLMs, checking another model’s answers, scoring against criteria. A filter before an expensive model: drop irrelevant passages from document search so the large model sees only what matters. A queue for human review: decide whether a person should look at a support agent’s conversation. This is one of the examples in the company’s evals. Evaluation at scale: an automatic judge for monitoring. The MLflow authors find Jev suitable for large-scale evaluation, but for debugging, where you need to understand the reason for a verdict, models that reason in text are better. The most realistic way to start, in my view, is a cascade: Jev handles what it is sure about, and the doubtful cases go to an expensive model or a person. Try it if: you have many repeated decisions every day latency is visible to your users you can split a decision into simple questions and test the result on your own data Wait if: you have few calls. On MLflow’s data, a million judgments a month cost about $25 with Jev and about $90 with Luna. In my view, for a small product that difference does not pay for the work of splitting the task into questions you need explanations for decisions, for example in a regulated industry the decision depends on math, code or long noisy text the text may contain someone else’s instruction and you have no second line of defense. In Braintrust’s test, one inserted instruction changed 12 to 22% of Jev’s answers your texts are not in English and you have not tested them. The documentation says English works best and other languages are handled but not equally well Early access has its own risks. The rate limits are 80 requests and 100,000 tokens per second right now, and the documentation warns that they can change without notice. The company also says it cannot prove its price is not subsidized. My experience I built a small Chrome extension for Polymarket with Claude Code and called it Ask Jev. You click a market card, the model gives its own probability without seeing the market price, and the extension stamps YES or NO next to the price. Every call goes into a log, so later I can see who was right more often, the model or the market. One thing to say plainly: it does not run on Jev. Jev was not in OpenRouter’s catalog when I built it, so the extension uses Gemini Flash with low reasoning effort. This is a story about a regular LLM doing the kind of job Jev is built for, not a test of Jev. The first version took 7.7 seconds per click. I measured inside the extension: the Polymarket API answered in 127 ms, and of 492 tokens in the model’s reply, 434 were thinking. Asking only about the two outcomes visible on the card instead of all of them, and lowering the reasoning effort, brought the median to 3.1 seconds over five clicks, with the best clicks at 1.9 to 2.2 seconds. Other models I tried took 11 to 44 seconds on a single test call. On the first live run, on a Fed rate decision market, the model gave 4% to the outcome the market priced at 67%, most likely because it reasons from what it remembers from training, not from the news. A few seconds for a yes or no probability is the gap Jev’s pitch is about: 70 to 500 milliseconds. I have not run Jev on this task, so I cannot say whether it closes that gap. Test it on your own data The best answer is your own measurement: Take 200 to 500 real cases from your logs where you know the right answer. Split the decision into 3 to 10 simple questions. Run the same set through Jev and through your current model. TypeSafe’s system-one-adapter-python helps: it accepts the same questions but answers with a regular LLM. Compare more than accuracy: price per thousand decisions, latency from your region, and above all the share of cases you can automate if you require, say, no more than 5% errors among them. The rest goes to the large model or a person. Setup Access is early. The playground and API keys are in the TypeSafe console, and the Classmethod author reports getting access right after joining the waitlist. Then install the Python SDK: pip install typesafe-sdk The client reads the key from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY environment variable. There is also a JavaScript SDK. Final thoughts Jev picks an option and gives a probability. It does not write text. “444 times cheaper” is the best case. Independent tests show about 4 to 27 times against small models. It is good at simple questions about meaning and weak at math and code. Split complex decisions into simple questions. The data is thin: small samples, synthetic emails, and a main benchmark written by the authors. Whether its probabilities can be trusted is still unproven. Test it on your own data before building anything critical on it. Where in your product does an LLM simply pick one option from a few? I would like to know how many such calls you have. If you enjoyed this article, I’d be grateful for your support I’m a Product Manager with an engineering background (ex SWE), focused on building, scaling and growing products. I’m especially interested in new technologies, particularly AI/ML, and how they can be applied in real workflows. Email: akzhankalimatov@gmail.com ✅ Connect with me on LinkedIn , X (Twitter) ✅ Press and hold the 👏 to give up to 50 claps for this article Sources TypeSafe Introducing System One Models & Jev , announcement and eval methodology Workflow evals Documentation: Quick start , Models , Jev 1.13 jaggedness system-one-adapter-python Independent sources The Register, Thomas Claburn, September 16 InfoWorld, Anirban Ghoshal, September 17 Phishing benchmark, anisselbd/jev-phishing-bench MLflow blog, Yuki Watanabe, September 22 Braintrust, Jev vs GPT eval judges, September 21 Classmethod, Jev for LLM model routing Every, Vibe Check: OpenAI DevDay 2026, Dan Shipper What Is Jev? What the Tests Show and Who Should Try It was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
A new model called Jev is built for this kind of job. You give it the ticket and the possible answers, and it returns a choice with a probability, nothing else. A startup called TypeSafe AI released it on September 15. The company says a response takes 70 to 500 milliseconds, and a million input tokens cost $0.042. Output tokens are free.

A note on how this article was made: I used Claude to help read the documentation, the announcement post and the independent tests, and to draft the text. All numbers come from the sources linked at the end. My own experience is in a separate section, “My experience”.

The same ticket, two ways to answer it.What it is

A regular LLM writes its answer one word at a time. Jev cannot do that. It reads a situation and a few questions, and returns numbers.

Think of a security guard at the door. The guard does not write a report. The guard decides in a second: let the person in, turn them away, or call a supervisor. Jev works the same way. There are three kinds of questions:

  • Choice: pick one option from a list, for example which team should handle a ticket.
  • Score: rate something on a scale you describe, for example how frustrated a customer is.
  • Noul: a yes or no question, for example whether a message is urgent.

Every answer comes with a probability. When the model is unsure, you can see it and send the case to a person or to a stronger model.

How it works

Here is an example from the documentation. A customer writes: “I’ve been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and the integration keeps failing. I’m losing sales. Please help ASAP.” You ask which team should handle it and whether it is urgent:

from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, TypeSafeClient
client = TypeSafeClient()  # reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY from the environment
ticket = "Hi, I've been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and the integration keeps failing. I'm losing sales. Please help ASAP."
response = client.system_one(
    state=ticket,
    questions={
        "department": Choice(
            instructions="Which team should handle this",
            criteria={
                "billing": "Payment or subscription issues",
                "technical": "Bugs or integration problems",
                "sales": "Pricing or account questions",
            },
        ),
        "is_urgent": Noul(
            instructions="The message conveys urgency or time-sensitivity",
        ),
    },
)
print(response.answers["department"].choice)  # "technical"
print(response.answers["is_urgent"].noul)     # 1.0

In the documentation’s example the answer is technical with 85% probability, billing 15%, sales 0%, and urgent: yes.

All questions go out in one request and are evaluated in parallel. That is where the speed comes from: the model does not write a long answer word by word. The company calls output tokens “too cheap to meter”, so they are free.

For Choice and Score answers you also get a confidence number from 0 to 1. You pick the threshold. In the documentation’s example, anything below 0.5 goes to a person.

A few things to know before your first request:

  • Input is text only. No images or audio.
  • There is one model for everyone. You cannot fine-tune it on your data, so you shape it with the wording of your questions.
  • The answer options must be defined in advance: a list, a scale or yes/no.
  • The name jev-latest points to the current version and changes with releases. If you tuned thresholds, pin the version number (it is 1.13.0 now).
What the tests show

It comes from the company’s own tests. If you recompute it from their table, 444.6 is the price of the most expensive model there (Opus 5) divided by the price of Jev. The authors themselves call these numbers the high end of real gains. Against small models the gain is smaller. In independent tests Jev was about 4 to 27 times cheaper and 2.6 to 23 times faster. That is still a lot.

Sources: evals.typesafe.ai, MLflow, Braintrust, jev-phishing-bench. Multiples marked ~ are approximate or calculated by the author from published figures.

Accuracy is the harder question, and there are only a few independent tests:

  • A phishing test on 2,000 synthetic on emails — on one general question, “is this phishing?”, Jev lost: 62.6% against 81.3% for Claude Haiku 4.5. Then the author split the task into five simple questions and combined the answers with a simple formula. Jev reached 95.0% and Haiku 93.2%, a tie on accuracy, but Jev was 27 times cheaper and 5 times faster. The author notes that the emails are synthetic and that the questions were written after studying the dataset.
  • MLflow (Databricks) — as a judge on 30 hand-labeled examples, Jev agreed with humans 30 times out of 30, like GPT-5.6 Terra and Luna. The median latency was 369 ms, and it cost $0.0247 per thousand judgments against $0.06 to $3.78 for the others. The sample is small, and the authors advise testing on your own data.
  • Braintrust — on checking whether a claim is supported by a source, Jev scored best at 80.2%, but the next model was at 79.2%, which is within noise. On judging whether an answer is correct it was weaker: 78.1% against 88.6% for Luna with reasoning, and 19 to 20 points behind on math and code.
  • Classmethod — an engineer tested Jev as the classifier of an LLM router with four difficulty levels, calling the API directly and not plugging it into the router. In 40 requests it picked the right level every time, at about 0.65 seconds per request. The classifiers in the original article took 2.1 and 7.2 seconds. The author does not call this a benchmark.

Jev does not replace a strong model. It answers simple questions fast and cheaply, especially when you split a complex decision into several simple ones.

What people say
  • David Linthicum, an independent consultant, told InfoWorld that many companies use a large LLM as a universal layer, even when the application only needs a quick choice from a few options. He sees Jev next to regular models: Jev for frequent simple decisions, the big model for reasoning and text.
  • Stephanie Walter of HyperFrame Research says developers will have to define questions, possible answers, thresholds and escalation paths in advance, which can be a lot of work, and that accuracy and calibration must be checked on your own data.
  • Paul Chada of Doozer AI points out that a probability shows how confident the model is, but not why. In regulated industries that is an audit problem.
  • Advait Patel of Broadcom says the approach could make control flow more explicit and easier to test, because the logic moves from prompts back into code. He also lists the risks of an early-stage vendor: security, data location, availability guarantees and dependency. The service currently runs in a single region.
  • The Register called the “zero hallucinations” claim an unfair comparison, because Jev does not write text and a structured answer can still be wrong.
  • Every reports that OpenAI previewed a Decisions API in late September with the same idea (context plus a fixed set of answers) and image input. The price is not announced. In Every’s informal tests, Decisions picked the right interface control in 76 of 78 steps against 73 for Jev. On classifying conversations, accuracy was about equal and Jev was faster: 161 ms against 309 ms.
Where it fits and who should try it

Where it fits:

  • Routing: where to send a customer request, or which model should handle a query. This is the case the Classmethod engineer tested.
  • First-line checks: guardrails for LLMs, checking another model’s answers, scoring against criteria.
  • A filter before an expensive model: drop irrelevant passages from document search so the large model sees only what matters.
  • A queue for human review: decide whether a person should look at a support agent’s conversation. This is one of the examples in the company’s evals.
  • Evaluation at scale: an automatic judge for monitoring. The MLflow authors find Jev suitable for large-scale evaluation, but for debugging, where you need to understand the reason for a verdict, models that reason in text are better.

The most realistic way to start, in my view, is a cascade: Jev handles what it is sure about, and the doubtful cases go to an expensive model or a person.

Try it if:

  • you have many repeated decisions every day
  • latency is visible to your users
  • you can split a decision into simple questions and test the result on your own data

Wait if:

  • you have few calls. On MLflow’s data, a million judgments a month cost about $25 with Jev and about $90 with Luna. In my view, for a small product that difference does not pay for the work of splitting the task into questions
  • you need explanations for decisions, for example in a regulated industry
  • the decision depends on math, code or long noisy text
  • the text may contain someone else’s instruction and you have no second line of defense. In Braintrust’s test, one inserted instruction changed 12 to 22% of Jev’s answers
  • your texts are not in English and you have not tested them. The documentation says English works best and other languages are handled but not equally well

Early access has its own risks. The rate limits are 80 requests and 100,000 tokens per second right now, and the documentation warns that they can change without notice. The company also says it cannot prove its price is not subsidized.

My experience

I built a small Chrome extension for Polymarket with Claude Code and called it Ask Jev. You click a market card, the model gives its own probability without seeing the market price, and the extension stamps YES or NO next to the price. Every call goes into a log, so later I can see who was right more often, the model or the market.

One thing to say plainly: it does not run on Jev. Jev was not in OpenRouter’s catalog when I built it, so the extension uses Gemini Flash with low reasoning effort. This is a story about a regular LLM doing the kind of job Jev is built for, not a test of Jev.

The first version took 7.7 seconds per click. I measured inside the extension: the Polymarket API answered in 127 ms, and of 492 tokens in the model’s reply, 434 were thinking. Asking only about the two outcomes visible on the card instead of all of them, and lowering the reasoning effort, brought the median to 3.1 seconds over five clicks, with the best clicks at 1.9 to 2.2 seconds. Other models I tried took 11 to 44 seconds on a single test call.

On the first live run, on a Fed rate decision market, the model gave 4% to the outcome the market priced at 67%, most likely because it reasons from what it remembers from training, not from the news.

A few seconds for a yes or no probability is the gap Jev’s pitch is about: 70 to 500 milliseconds. I have not run Jev on this task, so I cannot say whether it closes that gap.

Test it on your own data

The best answer is your own measurement:

  1. Take 200 to 500 real cases from your logs where you know the right answer.
  2. Split the decision into 3 to 10 simple questions.
  3. Run the same set through Jev and through your current model. TypeSafe’s system-one-adapter-python helps: it accepts the same questions but answers with a regular LLM.
  4. Compare more than accuracy: price per thousand decisions, latency from your region, and above all the share of cases you can automate if you require, say, no more than 5% errors among them. The rest goes to the large model or a person.
Setup

Access is early. The playground and API keys are in the TypeSafe console, and the Classmethod author reports getting access right after joining the waitlist. Then install the Python SDK:

pip install typesafe-sdk

The client reads the key from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY environment variable. There is also a JavaScript SDK.

Final thoughts
  • Jev picks an option and gives a probability. It does not write text.
  • “444 times cheaper” is the best case. Independent tests show about 4 to 27 times against small models.
  • It is good at simple questions about meaning and weak at math and code. Split complex decisions into simple questions.
  • The data is thin: small samples, synthetic emails, and a main benchmark written by the authors. Whether its probabilities can be trusted is still unproven.
  • Test it on your own data before building anything critical on it.

Where in your product does an LLM simply pick one option from a few? I would like to know how many such calls you have.

items.title: Meta was prepared to write an up to $200 billion AI check before knowing whether its model would work
items.summary: Zuckerberg said that in late 2025, Meta weighed a $200 billion AI bet before seeing its new models. Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance via Getty Images Zuckerberg said Meta weighed a $200 billion AI bet before seeing its new models. Alexandr Wang said Meta's CFO warned failure would be "very, very bad" financially. Meta's capex spending has been substantial and has raised eyebrows among investors Mark Zuckerberg was ready to bet as much as $200 billion on AI, and Meta’s finance chief wanted the person building it to understand what failure would mean. On the Cheeky Pint podcast released on Monday, Meta CEO and Alexandr Wang , Meta's chief AI officer, recounted conversations from late last year about enormous investments before Meta’s new models had proven themselves. “At the end of last year, we're like, all right, we are quite excited about the progress. We haven't seen the models yet,” Zuckerberg told show host John Collison. “I'm going to, like, you know, we're going to write this check for, like, I don't know, like $100 billion, $200 billion. I'm like, 'Alex, are you sure this is going to work?'” Zuckerberg said of Wang. Zuckerberg did not specify the timeframe or exact scope of that contemplated commitment. Wang said he had encouraging research updates at that point, but success was far from certain. At an executive gathering in Hawaii, Wang said that CFO Susan Li repeatedly pulled him aside. “Susan pulled me aside many times and was like, 'You know, I just want to tell you, if this doesn't work, like, you know, this is going to be really, really bad. It's going to be very, very bad in financial terms.'” Wang said of Li. Meta's capex over the past few quarters has been substantial, raising eyebrows among investors. Meta’s latest guidance puts 2026 capital expenditures, including finance lease principal payments, at $130 billion to $145 billion. In forecasts previously seen by Business Insider, Cantor Fitzgerald analysts expect the spending to reach $200 billion in 2027. Investors have shown limits. Meta shares fell more than 6% in after-hours trading following April’s earnings report, despite strong results, after the company raised its annual spending forecast to $125 billion to $145 billion. Inside Meta, the leadership is well aware of the stakes. In Wang's words, "this is a fuck ton of risk.” "So I think that in order for it not to work out, it's not just that we have to fail, AI overall has to fail," Zuckerberg said. "And then even if that happens, we still have all these other uses to productively use compute." Read the original article on Business Insider

Mark Zuckerberg was ready to bet as much as $200 billion on AI, and Meta’s finance chief wanted the person building it to understand what failure would mean.

On the Cheeky Pint podcast released on Monday, Meta CEO and Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, recounted conversations from late last year about enormous investments before Meta’s new models had proven themselves.

“At the end of last year, we're like, all right, we are quite excited about the progress. We haven't seen the models yet,” Zuckerberg told show host John Collison.

“I'm going to, like, you know, we're going to write this check for, like, I don't know, like $100 billion, $200 billion. I'm like, 'Alex, are you sure this is going to work?'” Zuckerberg said of Wang.

Zuckerberg did not specify the timeframe or exact scope of that contemplated commitment.

Wang said he had encouraging research updates at that point, but success was far from certain. At an executive gathering in Hawaii, Wang said that CFO Susan Li repeatedly pulled him aside.

“Susan pulled me aside many times and was like, 'You know, I just want to tell you, if this doesn't work, like, you know, this is going to be really, really bad. It's going to be very, very bad in financial terms.'” Wang said of Li.

Meta's capex over the past few quarters has been substantial, raising eyebrows among investors. Meta’s latest guidance puts 2026 capital expenditures, including finance lease principal payments, at $130 billion to $145 billion. In forecasts previously seen by Business Insider, Cantor Fitzgerald analysts expect the spending to reach $200 billion in 2027.

Investors have shown limits. Meta shares fell more than 6% in after-hours trading following April’s earnings report, despite strong results, after the company raised its annual spending forecast to $125 billion to $145 billion.

Inside Meta, the leadership is well aware of the stakes. In Wang's words, "this is a fuck ton of risk.”

"So I think that in order for it not to work out, it's not just that we have to fail, AI overall has to fail," Zuckerberg said. "And then even if that happens, we still have all these other uses to productively use compute."

items.title: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
items.summary: Autoregressive decoding is less suited to non-causally ordered data, e.g., cross-references or future dependencies, since their outputs cannot be revised post hoc, unlike iterative human reasoning. Diffusion LLMs partially mitigate this limitation but still cannot flexibly insert or remove arbitrary numbers of tokens from a pre-generated context. We design AutoIndexer as a generative model with a novel training and decoding mechanism that simulates a Chain of Edits, allowing the model to flexibly modify its prior outputs in hindsight via token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model learns to predict marker tokens for opening and closing edits, simultaneously moving a cursor to positions in the existing token sequence, analogous to a text editor. Training sequences are obtained by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to edit by undoing those inverses. The perturbation training allows AutoIndexer to be robust to erroneous context and adaptable to editing tasks such as code correction. We demonstrate that our method exhibits post-generation context-editing capabilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/autoindexer.

items.title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
items.summary: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.

items.title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Draftsfor Speculative Decoding
items.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by the target model. Recent diffusion-based drafters make this paradigm particularly attractive: deep attention-based neural backbones provide strong predictions, while drafting multiple future positions in parallel avoids the sequential cost of autoregressive generation. This parallelism, however, comes at a cost. Tokens within a draft block are predicted without access to the realized identities of preceding draft tokens, removing intra-block dependencies that would naturally be available under autoregressive generation. We introduce DCOCO (DFlash Contextual Corrector), a lightweight mechanism that restores these dependencies while preserving parallel drafting. Rather than committing to each position's top prediction, DCOCO retains multiple candidate tokens and evaluates their contextual compatibility across adjacent draft positions in parallel, enabling contextually informed token selection at low additional cost. Across four verifier backbones and ten benchmarks, DCOCO achieves the highest average throughput in every evaluated configuration, spanning greedy and stochastic decoding with and without extended reasoning, with speedups of up to 6.6x over vanilla decoding. Its advantage persists under concurrent serving: DCOCO outperforms the strongest competing method by 6-23% across 4-32 concurrent requests, while other sequential correctors fall below uncorrected DFlash at these loads. These results demonstrate that recovering intra-block dependencies through parallel contextual scoring delivers consistent acceleration across decoding regimes and serving loads.

items.title: CLUE: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Unsupervised Event Type Induction and Annotation
items.summary: Event ontology is the foundational framework for defining events in a dataset. Event type induction generally involves domain experts who define guidelines for creating event types and their names based on the dataset's domain and scope. However, this process is resource-intensive in terms of annotation costs and is prone to human biases. To alleviate the need for manual event ontology creation, we propose the CLUE framework for event type induction, naming, and annotation. Our main contributions in this work are: 1) designing a novel joint embedding representation for expressing both the verb-centric view and the semantic view of events; 2) event type induction using contrastive loss guided clustering; 3) event naming and refinement. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at https://github.com/PratikMaitra/CLUE.

items.title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models
items.summary: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.

items.title: Reflective Prompt Optimization of a Deep-Research Agent: A Topic-Disjoint, Multi-Seed Protocol for Measuring Transferable Gains and Prompt-Level Overfitting
items.summary: Prompt optimization is an attractive alternative to reinforcement learning for adapting language-model agents, since it is cheap and produces human-readable artifacts. On factual tasks, however, it carries a failure mode that scalar-reward reinforcement learning does not. An optimizer that reads the training examples can write their answers into the prompt, so an in-distribution gain may be memorization rather than transferable behaviour. We apply reflective prompt evolution (GEPA) to the two system prompts of a multi-agent deep-research agent and evaluate it under a topic-disjoint split in which no topic is shared across train, validation, and test. Held-out citation reward rises by 0.079, from 0.702 to 0.781, with a bootstrap 95\% confidence interval of [0.051, 0.107], and the gain replicates across three seeds (mean 0.107). Nearly half of the winning prompt is a memorized answer key, yet a controlled ablation shows this content earns no reward even on the exact training questions it encodes. The large validation-minus-held-out gap is therefore small-sample selection under a noisy judge, not memorization. Varying the verifier isolates what makes the gain transfer. Decomposed per-dimension feedback is the causal ingredient, and collapsing it to a single scalar reward makes held-out transfer negative. The gain persists under an out-of-family judge and is largely reproduced by a hand-written version of the discovered recipe. Credible evaluation of prompt optimizers therefore requires held-out topics, multiple seeds, and verifier ablations. We release the candidate prompts, lineage diffs, figures, tables, and analysis.

items.title: Self-Preservation in Language Models
items.summary: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.

To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.

items.title: GeopoliticalQA: Benchmarking Retrieval and Generation over Intelligence Reports
items.summary: Geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports constitute a rich source of expert knowledge and have increasing value in the current political climate, but their heterogeneity and analytical complexity pose challenges for retrieval-augmented question answering. We introduce a benchmark for grounded question answering over 415 open-source geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports, comprising 5,525 document-grounded question-answer pairs spanning factual, inferential, comparative, and risk-oriented questions. We propose a document-aware generation pipeline that profiles reports before generating questions and validate dataset quality through expert annotation and an LLM-as-judge protocol. Using the benchmark, we evaluate 15 retrieval systems and six open-weight LLMs for RAG. We find that models perform similarly on document-level retrieval, while at the harder chunk level retrieval quality is not driven by embedding-model scale: bge-m3, a mid-size open encoder matches an order of magnitude larger ones and outperforms commercial embedding APIs. In contrast, answer generation remains challenging even given the gold evidence, particularly for inferential and risk-oriented questions.

items.title: perturber: A Stateless Service for Semantics-Preserving Text Perturbations
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) evaluations on clean benchmarks overstate model robustness: real inputs arrive perturbed, and these meaning-preserving variants routinely move model answers. Studying this systematically requires applying perturbations one at a time, reproducibly, and identically wherever they run, yet existing tools couple them to a benchmarking stack rather than packaging them as a reusable transform layer. We present perturber, a stateless service and Python library that applies exactly one semantics-preserving perturbation per call, drawn from a first-party catalog of 68 perturbations across 11 families. It turns on a single primitive, with composition left to the caller chaining calls, so the service and the library produce identical output by construction. We evaluate the tool itself, its correctness, reproducibility, and cost, rather than any model's robustness, measuring meaning-preservation per perturbation rather than assuming it. The demonstration adds a live playground, an introspectable catalog for benchmark selection, and a one-command reproducible evaluation.

items.title: GeoFitBench-LLM: A Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Capabilities in Geospatial Data Requirements Elicitation for Geo-Analytic Tasks
items.summary: Large language models are becoming central to GeoAI systems, yet their evaluation rarely considers the elicitation of geospatial data requirements. This omission is critical as retrieval oriented geo-analytic tasks cannot be supported reliably without first identifying the necessary datasets and constraints. GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark for assessing whether LLMs can infer the datasets, the supporting resources and the constraints required by geo-analytic requests in natural language. The benchmark is structured around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, reflecting long-standing challenges in geospatial information retrieval and related natural language tasks. Ground truth requirements are encoded in a fixed, provider-independent schema for reproducible evaluation of resource identification and attribute-level specification. Experiments on seven models under minimal prompting indicate that identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with GPT-5.4 Thinking achieving the best result by recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of benchmark requests. Results further indicate that accurate fitness-for-use specification remains more difficult as inferential demands increase.

items.title: Activating the Annotator: Operationalising Lived Experience in Data Annotation
items.summary: Perspectivist NLP has established that annotator positionality shapes labels for subjective tasks, but the field still lacks methods for operationalising it. Positionality is typically operationalised as a demographic form completed at recruitment: a static attribute recorded once and treated as a covariate, on the assumption that the knowledge it indexes is active when the annotator reads an item. This paper treats that assumption as a design problem and asks whether lived experience can instead be primed by the task itself. We introduce AXLE, a pre-annotation stage in which a scenario vignette anchors a short, axis-guided conversation that is synthesised into a first-person micro-narrative and returned to the annotator before labelling begins. In a 2x2 between-subjects study (104 annotators, 30 items, 1,040 annotations) on ambiguous hate speech spanning immigration, religion and gender, elicitation was associated with higher identity resonance and higher sensitivity to harm. It also increased label entropy and lowered inter-annotator agreement: the stage appears to surface plurality rather than manufacture consensus, which distinguishes it from annotator training, whose success criterion is convergence.

items.title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
items.summary: Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy's own verifier-labeled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark. Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations, and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.

items.title: U4RASD at KnowledgeGraphEval-2026: Ontology-Constrained Encoder and LLM Systems for Arabic Relation Extraction
items.summary: This paper details our submission to KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 Subtask 2 on directed Arabic relation extraction. We explored encoder-based and large language model approaches for predicting one of 40 relations or no_relation from an Arabic sentence and a subject-object pair. Our encoder systems use typed entity markers and separate relation-existence and relation-classification heads, while our LLM systems fine-tune Yehia and Qwen3.5 with QLoRA and ontology-constrained prediction. Our best system, an ensemble of Yehia-RE, Qwen-RE, and TypedPair, achieved a micro-F1 score of 94.06 and ranked 1st in Subtask 2. Yehia-RE (full-vocabulary) achieved 92.98, while the best encoder and Qwen-RE achieved 92.69 and 91.94 respectively. Our results highlight the importance of constrained prediction and complementary modeling approaches for Arabic relation extraction.

items.title: MADS: Multi-Agent Dialog Simulation for Robust Conversational Agents
items.summary: Task-oriented conversational agents remain fragile under realistic conditions, especially when users exhibit non-cooperative behavior. Existing function-calling benchmarks underrepresent adversarial conversation trajectories, thereby limiting the training resources available for developing robust agents. We present MADS (Multi-Agent Dialog Simulation), a synthetic data generation pipeline that produces structured, diverse dialogue trajectories. We inject adversarial conversation, producing validated conversation trajectories that capture realistic, unhappy paths. Using MADS, we construct MADS-Bench: a benchmark spanning six domains, 55 personas, and 1095 conversations, with approximately 66% of conversations containing failure-prone conversation scenarios. We evaluate the robustness of the trained models using a two-stage training approach that combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
